speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Privatization)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today pursuant to Standing Order 19(6) and as Minister responsible for regulatory affairs to inform the House of an important milestone in the implementation of the Government's regulatory reform strategy. Hon. Members will recall that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) identified regulatory reform as an important contributor to economic growth and job creation when he announced the Government's agenda for economic renewal in November 1984.
The Government subsequently developed a comprehensive regulatory reform strategy as a result of the work of the Ministerial task force on program review. The strategy and our smarter regulation policy were announced in February. Since then, there has been virtually constant action in the Government to bring about needed and practical improvements in regulatory programs and the federal regulatory system.
Regulation is the use of law to control or prohibit private behaviour. A democratically elected Parliament is recognized as the source of those laws and of regulations affecting the freedom of all the people. It follows that Parliament has a special responsibility in encouraging sound, practical regulatory reform.
Of course, a major purpose of the regulatory plan is to respond still further to the Government's commitment to open
Government. The document gives the public early notice of our intentions and this will help individuals to influence reglation at the start and not just at the end of the regulatory pipeline.
[ Translation]
That is why I see it as especially appropriate to announce in the House today that we are releasing, simultaneously with this statement, the first annual regulatory plan prepared by a federal Government.
The regulatory plan for 1987 provides a comprehensive list of regulatory initiatives planned by 25 federal Departments and agencies for next year.
It is the result of the introduction of compulsory planning and priority setting introduced to the federal regulatory system as a result of the regulatory reform strategy. Because it covers all planned federal regulatory activity during a specific 12-month planning period and because it has been approved by Cabinet as a planning document, the 1987 regulatory plan goes well beyond the scope and objectives of the old regulatory agendas.

In the same spirit, I see the annual plan becoming a very useful reference document for Members of Parliament. Copies of the 1987 plan are being circulated at this time to Members' offices as well as copies of an information kit prepared to accompany the plan's release.
One of my main objectives has been to ensure that the plan is a useful tool for Members of Parliament and I hope they will let me have any suggestions on how we can improve next year's edition. This is a good example of how the smarter regulation policy is producing practical, helpful improvements that have long been needed.

Mr. Speaker, I was asked to act as Liberal critic on this matter because I happen to be co-chairman of the Joint Committee on Regulations. That is why my reply will not be as charitable as the Minister may have wished.

I have to say that I am interested in this document but I cannot receive it with the kind of enthusiasm with which the Minister has delivered it. It is not all that different from the regulatory agenda approach introduced years ago by my colleauge, the Hon. Member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) when he was the President of the Treasury Board. Like that document, the trouble with this document is that it is not a law

December 15, 1986

of Canada. It is not a regulation. It has no status or authority, other than a commitment by the Government to comply with it. In other words, any Department will continue to be free to put out regulations whenever it likes. Those regulations will stand or fall, not in relation to this plan but in relation to the law.
[DOT] (mo)
I regret that after the commitment the Government made to the regulatory reform process that it has not been prepared to do something that will have more authority than justify a statement. I hope that it will not unduly encumber the process of Departments, and that in cases where regulations have very little consequence that those regulations will be able to go forward and will not be encumbered by all this material, which although it is well intended, has to be characterized as additional red tape for departments. It is red tape that could produce good results. I do wish to indicate that it is not always a good thing, unless it is applied with sensitivity and taken seriously by the departments.
I am suspicious about the commitment of the Government to regulatory reform because of the behaviour of the Government and its caucus in relation to the regulatory process. This is a good time to mention it, because the Government wants the country to accept this document and to see it as a reform. Since it has no legal authority, it will only have meaning if the Government is committed to it.
These are the reasons that the Government has very little commitment to regulatory reform. First, it has not yet acted to amend the Statutory Instruments Act. In 1983 when Mark MacGuigan was the Minister of Justice he made a commitment that the Statutory Instruments Act would be amended. It has no teeth, it has no disallowance power, and no one was more enthusiastic about Mr. MacGuigan's commitment than the Opposition. So all of this regulatory process could be effectively controlled by a regulatory instruments process. No amendments have been introduced to carry that out.
Second, the attendance of Conservative members at the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and other Statutory Instruments has prevented us from doing our job. Four meetings have been called with two Liberal members, one NDP member, nine Conservative members-

My third point in challenging the credibility of this Government as a regulatory reformer is the behaviour of the Minister's former Department when she was Minister of State for Finance in dealing with regulations which we brought to the attention of the Government that challenged its constitutional authority. The committee has the responsibility of reviewing regulations. Although I could have mentioned several, I have mentioned the Hon. Minister's Department because she is charged now with the SOR/82-359, the Natural Gas and Gas Liquids Tax Regulation.
On December 5, 1984, our legal counsel wrote to the Department asking them to respond to a challenge to a regulation to its authority. There was no reply to the letter. On April 10, 1985, we wrote again. A committee of Parliament wrote to the Minister's Department and did not even receive the courtesy of a reply saying that our letter would be looked into.
The first letter was on December 5, 1984, the second letter was on April 10, 1985, the third letter was on August 20, and there was not even the courtesy of a reply from the Minister's Department. On January 2, 1986 our legal counsel wrote and again there was no reply. On April 17, 1986 the co-chairman of the committee and the vice-chairman wrote to the Minister asking for a reply to all these letters that had been written. There was no reply. On September 17, 1986 we wrote again and asked the Government to deal with, in our view, a breach of the regulations and there was no reply. So these are the reformers. I will believe it when I see it.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words on the statement by the Minister. They will be very few because the spokesman for the New Democratic Party on this particular issue had a prior commitment. We did not receive notice of this from the Minister's office or a statement ahead of time. I am not sure whether it was the Minister's office that was late in sending it, or whether the confusion resulted on our side. Maybe it was Canada Post. But we have not received notice of it. The Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) is our spokesman on this particular issue and he has other commitments at this time.
I wish to say to the Minister that we follow this issue. It is an important issue for people. We know about the committee that has been going on. The only point that I wish to make this
December 15, 1986

morning is that this issue of regulatory reform is an issue which we should make sure works on behalf of the average Canadian who is affected by the laws of Canada. There will always be regulations. There will always be reform and update of regulations, regardless of which Government is in power. There must be a process that ensures that the regulations of Government work on behalf of ordinary citizens. All too often the ordinary citizen is met with red tape, regulations, and guidelines that are beyond his or her comprehension. They tend to see parliamentarians and public servants, particularly at the federal level in Ottawa, drafting very complicated regulations that can only be interpreted by lawyers, or accountants, and sometimes for the benefit of lawyers and accountants.
It is encumbent upon all of us in the three Parties in the House to make sure that the regulations are drafted in the most efficient and effective way possible that work and serve ordinary Canadians.

People are the most important factor. There are Canadian men and women across this country who have to work with federal Government programs, any programs. We have a policy for farmers, a policy for fishermen, a welfare policy, there are Old Age Security pensions, just about anything, Mr. Speaker. But the main thing is to communicate with Canadians across this country.

It is very important in any reform process that we have input from ordinary people, and from their organizations and associations.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Statements by Ministers. The Hon. President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret).

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 5, 1986, I indicated that, further to the request of my colleague, the Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Kelleher), I was asking that a review be made of the circumstances which surrounded the award of the Port-Cartier project direction contract to Bechtel Quebec Ltd. The request for such a review followed allegations that the Code of Conflict of Interest may have been breached. This review has been completed. The following facts were brought to my attention.
In July, 1985 Correctional Services appointed Mr. Robert McCulloch, then at the service of Correctional Services, interim project director for the Port-Cartier project. Robert McCulloch was a Bechtel Canada employee, working in the
Statements by Ministers
public service by way of an Interchange Canada agreement. Since this agreement was coming to an end, it was decided to retain the services of Robert McCulloch by contract.
A request was forwarded to Bechtel Canada Limited to prepare a proposal which would be relied upon to draft a project direction contract. Correctional Services attempted to enter into a sole source agreement with Bechtel. This attempt was not accepted, and the Department of Supply and Services required that requests for proposals be sought.

In December 1985, the Minister of Supply and Services invited thirteen companies to submit proposals. Eight, including Bechtel, responded. After an analysis of the proposals, three out of eight were retained for consideration, including Bechtel. The latter company was awarded the contract because its proposal was judged to be the best and least costly. An analysis of the circumstances of the entire process has shown that once the decision was made to go ahead with the construction of a penitentiary institution within a relatively short time frame, the flexibility required to develope a work plan and policies was somewhat reduced.
Mr. McCulloch should not have been appointed as acting director for the project since it was known that he would not be able to perform those duties up to the project's completion.

The analysis further indicates that Robert McCulloch's status, for example, a senior Bechtel employee and Correctional Services officer, placed him in a conflict of interest situation as soon as it was determined that Bechtel was to be requested to prepare a proposal which would lead to a contract. Robert McCulloch should then have been removed from both the project and the contracting process which would lead to a contract with the firm, Bechtel.
Robert McCulloch who, by the term of his Interchange agreement, was subject to the Conflict of Interest Code, and senior Correctional Services employees should have been more concerned about the conflict of interest situation which existed, particularly since in September, 1985, when these events were unfolding, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) tabled in the House a Conflict of Interest Code, which code was introducing clearer and tougher rules.
I have asked my colleague, the Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher), to require the Correctional Services Commissioner, Rheal Leblanc, to examine carefully the facts which surround the matter and take such measures as he feels are needed to deal with it.
I have also asked my colleague, the Hon. Minister of Supply and Services (Mrs. Vezina), who has accepted, to terminate the contract between Robert McCulloch, Bechtel, and the Crown in the public interest.

December 15, 1986
Statements by Ministers
The Solicitor General will also be taking the necessary steps to provide for the continuation of project direction through the offices of Correctional Services and Public Works Canada.
The decision to terminate the contract is consistent with the Government's commitment with respect to the Conflict of Interest Code.

Mr. Speaker, I should first like to indicate that the Official Opposition was only provided with a copy of the Minister's statement literally minutes ago. It would seem to me that there should be some common courtesies in the House. Where statements are to be delivered by Ministers, they should be given to opposition Parties in advance, in order to give opposition Parties an opportunity to assess properly the statements to be made. I hope the Minister will recognize the difficult position in which he puts the Official Opposition in trying to respond to as important a statement as the one made by the Minister. Be that as it may, I will attempt to respond to the statement of the Minister.
It is obvious from what the Minister stated that there has been a conflict of interest, that rules and regulations were not followed in this particular case. We in the Opposition have indicated from the start that an investigation was necessary into the whole question of the prison in the riding of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).
The Auditor General indicated that $41 million of taxpayers' money was literally frittered away because of the Prime Minister's desire to locate the prison in Manicouagan, his riding. The Prime Minister, through Ministers of the Crown, indicated on a number of occasions that there was a need for a prison in Port-Cartier, notwithstanding the fact that the Auditor General concluded there was no such need for a protective custody prison in Manicouagan. Despite the statements of the Auditor General, the Government continued to insist that in fact there was a need. In effect, the Government, through various Ministers of the Crown, called in question the objectivity and the independence of the Auditor General. It was unprecedented in the history of the Office of the Auditor General for Ministers of the Crown to attack the Auditor General with regard to his objectivity and with regard to his independence.
I see you signalling, Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: One minute.
With the leave of the House, I would ask for the opportunity to complete my comments.
No.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I am allowing the Hon. Member an extra minute to complete his comments.

Perhaps I will have to make comments at another time. However, the bottom line is that there has been a conflict of interest. They are holding Mr. McCulloch
responsible; they are making a scapegoat of him. In fact the Minister should be held responsible and the Minister should resign. If not, the conflict of interest guidelines are a farce.
They are saying that Mr. McCulloch was responsible for putting himself in a conflict of interest situation. I suggest that it is the Prime Minister who put Mr. McCulloch and Bechtel in a conflict of interest situation by insisting a prison go in his riding and by insisting that the contract be completed by September, 1988. It is the Minister's resignation which is needed, not simply the termination of the contract. This leads me to another point-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I regret to inform the Hon. Member that his time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, it was obviously the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who gave directions to go full speed ahead with the plan for a penitentiary at Port-Cartier, without regard for the consequences.
The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) has now recognized the existence of a conflict of interest that was pointed out here in the House. However, he has not blamed the Prime Minister, although it was the Prime Minister's insistence on this project-despite the cost and despite the fact that all Government tendering practices would be and were adhered to-that created this situation.

I recall to Hon. Members of the House that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) decided he wanted to have this prison as a bon-bon to give to the people of Port-Cartier. It is clear that Port-Cartier would prefer to have real development, development which provided a variety of jobs, not just prison guard jobs. However, when it was decided in the first place, he incurred an estimated $41 million in extra costs because of the relocation of the prison from Drummondville. The report of the Auditor General indicated that it would have been $10 million cheaper to have renovated the prison in Laval rather than to move it to Drummondville.
The Government decided to move at full speed and damn the consequences. It is now turning around and making a statement that poor Mr. McCulloch is to blame, that he should have realized there was a conflict of interest and should have kept out of it when he was asked if he would please stay on for a few months at the end of his Interchange Canada contract in order to get the project under way. It seems that the Government should have understood that if it were asking this particular official, who had been in Government for a very short period of time on an Interchange contract, it should have looked at the question of conflict of interest.
To blame the Commissioner of Correctional Services, Mr. Rheal Leblanc, for the fact that the contract was not put forward correctly and that there was a conflict of interest also begs the real question-why was the Government going at such a pace? We know the reason. It was because the Prime



December 15, 1986

Minister wanted to cut the blue ribbon on the project before a possible election in May or June, 1988. That was the reason. It was a politically motivated project. The Government now finds that it has egg on its face. However, I welcome the fact that it has decided to put on the brakes in terms of the particular contract.
I want to tell the people at Bechtel Canada that I regret their having been drawn into this matter for reasons I do not believe were their responsibility at all. I think that a private sector company has been ill served by the Government which put political priorities ahead of doing business in the ordinary way that the Government should, namely, in a way in which the bidding process is fair, above board and gives a fair chance to everybody. If Bechtel's bid was the lowest bid, then in the normal course of events it should have been awarded the contract. The fact that a conflict of interest emerged was not Bechtel's fault, was not Mr. McCulloch's fault, it was the Government's fault because Brian Mulroney wanted that prison in Port Cartier.

Mr. Speaker, as was indicated, the purpose of Bill C-31 is to extend for six months the Farm Improvement Loans Act. The Act has always contained a sunset clause. The initial period of the Act was three years, and it has been extended since then, from time, to time usually for three-year intervals. This has provided an opportunity to reconsider the provisions of the Act and amend it as necessary to ensure that it continues to meet the needs of Canadian farmers.
The last extension of this Act involved the period of 18 months from July 1, 1985 to December 31, 1986. It was our intention to carry out a full review of the program during that 18-month period so that we would be in a position to propose needed amendments to make it more useful and then extend it for a longer period of time.
Substantial work has been done on this review. However, the need to deal with some very serious financial problems facing farmers has made it impossible to complete the review and the necessary consultations with farm organizations and lenders across the country. It is because of the need to provide additional time to complete the review and the necessary consultations that I seek an amendment to the Act which will

December 15, 1986

extend my authority to guarantee new loans for an additional six months.
Over the course of the review it has become apparent that in some ways the Act has indeed achieved many of its original objectives. When the program was first introduced some 41 years ago, in 1945, there was little mid-term credit available to farmers from commercial lenders. Between 1945 and the middle-1960s a very substantial part of the credit provided to farmers was guaranteed under this Act. In the late 1960s and through the 1970s the use of the program declined as commercial lenders introduced their own loan programs for farmers. The decline in the number and dollar amounts of loans extended under the Act continued into the 1980s as the serious financial difficulties facing agriculture caused farmers to cut back on their investment in farm machinery, equipment and buildings. Despite that decline, the program continues to occupy a small but very significant place in the field of agricultural credit. In 1985, the last year for which figures are available, there were just under 12,000 loans extended for a total amount of SI65 million.
While this program occupies only a relatively small part of the over-all agricultural credit field, it is important to remember that it is only one part of the over-all contribution of the federal Government to the credit needs of Canadian farmers. The Farm Credit Corporation has long played a major role in long-term agricultural credit. With the serious financial difficulties facing farmers we have strengthened that role by taking such special measures as reducing the rate of interest paid by farmers locked into high interest rate loans and by introducing new financial instruments such as a shared risk mortgage and Commodity-based Loan Program. We have also strengthened and extended existing agricultural credit programs such as the small business bond, the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act and the Advance Payments for Crops Act. We also introduced a system of Farm Debt Review Boards to help farmers in financial difficulty reach settlements with their creditors. All of these initiatives have helped farmers obtain the credit they need in a period of serious financial distress.
At the same time, the initiatives taken in agricultural credit are but a small part of the total assistance we have provided to farmers in a period when external forces have created very serious difficulties for many farmers in this country. These initiatives have ranged from steps taken to effectively offset all federal sales and excise taxes on farm fuels to the $1 billion special Canada grains program that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) announced December 9.
When the review of this Act was carried out, suggestions were made that a radical restructuring is not really needed. However, additional work and consultation is necessary to verify this view and identify the adjustment and changes which need to be made if the Act is to continue to fulfil its role in the agricultural credit field. Again, the review is not yet complete but the consultations we have had with farm groups suggest there is basic support for the program and a recognition that
Farm Improvement Loans Act
some adjustment may be necessary to ensure its continued contribution to Canadian agriculture. Indeed, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture indicated its support for the program and recommended there be a short extension to permit additional time for the review and consultation to be completed.
With the passage of this Act it is my intention to complete the review as quickly as possible and introduce substantive amendments early in the new year. That will ensure ample time for deliberations on the amendments by Parliament before the six-month extension period expires. Therefore I urge my colleagues, indeed all Hon. Members of this House, to support the Bill so that we can meet the needs of Canadian farmers during that interval.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to speak on Bill C-31. While the Minister has yet to get his act together concerning exactly how he is going to amend the Bill, at least the uncertainty which has reigned supreme in this country since September 26, when a press report indicated the Government might be cancelling the program, has ended. We learned last Thursday or Friday that the Government was going to extend the program for another six months at least. I take it from the Minister's comments this morning that he may actually continue the program in the future and improve it. That is encouraging since the farm debt crisis facing Canadian agricultural since the fall of 1984 is one area where the Government has failed to take any very effective action.
Just about $3 billion, that is all.

We have seen a lot of hype about what the Government is going to do but we have not seen very much action. That is of great concern because during the 1984 election campaign the Government committed itself to allocating the necessary funds to assist producers in refinancing their loans at prevailing rates of interest. The amended Farm Improvement Loans Act might be useful in that regard because the rate of interest is 1 per cent above prime.
[DOT] (USO)
In 1979, 25,309 loans were granted under this program for total financial assistance of $265 million. In 1984 only half as many loans, 12,000 were granted for total financial assistance of $159 million. We on this side of the House wonder why so little is being made available to farmers. Perhaps the Minister will explain in Committee of the Whole why the Government is leaving us uncertain as to whether or not it is phasing the program out and why the funds seem to be unavailable.
The FCC is the important funding agency of the federal Government. Thirty-two per cent of its inventory of loans is outstanding at interest rates of between 12.75 per cent and
16.75	per cent. That seems to fly in the face of the Government's campaign commitment that it would reschedule loans to current interest rates. The Government found funding in the FCC in 1984 which allowed it to reschedule some loans to

Farm Improvement Loans Act
12.75	per cent. Farmers who would swear that they were going broke had their loans rescheduled from 14 per cent and up to
12.75 per cent. It is hard to say what would have happened had there not been $575 million left in the FCC funding account in the fall of 1984.
There has been great uncertainty as to whether the Government was going to renew this program. A report in The Globe and Mail of September 26 said that there was millions at stake for cash-starved farmers and that the axe may fall on farm and fishing loan schemes. At that time the Minister obviously did not have a commitment from the Government to continue this program. He issued a press release on October 6 in which he said that he considered it a priority for Canadian farmers to have access to adequate credit. However, he did not really clarify until last Friday whether the axe would fall on this legislation.
That type of uncertainty is exactly what our agricultural community does not want. We did not know for certain until a week ago whether the Government was going to proceed with its special grain program for western Canada. The Opposition, the prairie pools and other groups have been calling upon the Government to provide assistance of between $2 billion and $4 billion a year. Finally last Tuesday the Minister and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) announced that they were going to make the payment. However, they are going to spread it out over such a period of time that many farmers who are facing financial crises right now will not receive assistance until next April or May. In fact, farmers on average will receive only $1,500 in January or February. The $3,500 balance of assistance under that program will not be received until next April or May. For the 39,000 farmers in serious financial difficulty that assistance will come so late that it will be questionable how much help it will be.
This assistance, however, is more real than the announcement made by the Prime Minister last April 30 of $300 million or $400 million of so-called assistance, which resulted in no assistance at all because most farmers received very little from it. That program was supposed to freeze freight rates. However, it turned out that it was only a recalculation of the volume of freight rates. There was no real saving of $42 million. It was only a smoke and mirrors operation.
The Minister also implied that the Government was going to increase the domestic price of wheat from $7 to $11. In fact, it was only increasing the range. Farmers had expected a $200 million to $300 million benefit from that. He announced with great flourish that on May 1 he would remove the 2-cent a litre excise tax which he had imposed in September of 1985. He expected everyone to cheer. They did not cheer. In fact, most farmers wanted to know why the Government had imposed this 2-cent a litre tax which cost farmers $60 million or $70 million when farmers were already in serious financial difficulty. Why would any Government which was serious about helping farmers do that in the first place?
In addition, there has been tremendous uncertainty about the free trade negotiations. We wonder what kind of deal
Simon Reisman will make in the dark of the night. We wonder whether he will trade away our marketing and stabilization programs. This week 50 or 60 farmers are coming to Ottawa to find out whether the Government will make the final payment on No. 1 and No. 2 wheat. There is a precedent for the Government making that final payment as it did for durum wheat in 1969-70. Farmers want to know why that $190 or $200 million payment will not be made directly to them. I am sure the Minister will change his mind and make that final payment which will be so beneficial to farmers, especially in view of the fact that he has delayed it for many months.
We are also interested in knowing why the Government is not extending the moratorium on FCC loans for the same time that it is procrastinating in making the final payment on the special grains program. I can hear the Minister saying that he has not lifted the moratorium; perhaps in Committee of the Whole he will be able to announce that he will extend the moratorium on FCC foreclosures for another few months.
Let us consider the Government's financial assistance to farmers. During this Fiscal year it is providing some $65 million for the farm debt crisis, the largest proportion of which is for the Canadian Rural Transition Program which is designed to take farmers off the farm. Some $20 million is going to that program, some $10 million for the Farm Debt Review Board and the actual financial assistance for the FCC to write down loans is only $10 million. The Provinces of Ontario, Saskatchewan and Alberta are providing a great deal more proportionately.
There is some $20 million allocated to the commodity-based mortgage for the reduction of interest rates, but when we read the fine print we see that over the ten-year life of those mortgages most farmers will in fact not only pay back all of that $20 million of interest that has been allocated, they will end up paying some 12.75 per cent interest on that program. The Government itself makes it clear in its advertisements that this is not a subsidy program and there is no assistance really available unless the value of the commodity stays extremely low.
In spite of all our misgivings about the Government's plans and the uncertainty about whether the Government will renew or hopefully improve the program for farmers who make use of it, we believe that the Bill should be passed and the life of the program extended. When we get to Committee of the Whole I will want to know why this program is not used in many parts of the country, such as in Ontario where a very small percentage of these loans are approved. Farmers are often paying from 12 per cent to 15 per cent interest, when a program such as this is available. I hope the Minister is prepared to make a commitment to ensure that the chartered banks make adequate funds available, as was promised in the 1984 general election.
December 15, 1986

In conclusion, we are prepared to pass the Bill today and see the life of the Farm Improvement Loans Act extended for another six months.
Mir. Vic Althouse (Humboldt-Lake Centre): Mr. Speaker, the Bill we are debating today is an interim measure by which the Minister can extend the life of the Farm Improvement Loans Act for another six months. The Minister has been facing a dilemma regarding the Farm Improvement Loans Act and, like all dilemmas, it has two horns. First, shortly after the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) took office he had consultations with his various provincial counterparts and their Deputy Ministers. He was told in 1984 that the Farm Improvement Loans Act should be continued, but with some changes. Among those changes that were proposed was that the rate of interest be fixed as it was when the Act was originally introduced. Furthermore, these fixed rates should continue from one to five years and the Government's guarantees for the loans and the other aspects of the program should continue.
Faced with that proposal, which I support, he has also been faced with the proposal by the Nielsen Task Force which looked at the Farm Improvement Loans Act and said: "The study team recommends to the task force that the Government consider allowing the program to expire and transfer the administration of the claims payment to the Farm Credit Corporation". The Minister has had to deal with this conflicting advice and I believe we should examine those choices in this debate.
Since 1945 farmers have used the Farm Improvement Loans Act which has extended loans of various amounts. The program had been renewed every three years until it expired on June 30, 1985, when the Minister decided to extend it until the end of 1986. If we did not pass this Bill to extend the Farm Improvement Loans Act for another six months, it would cease at the end of this month. It is unclear what would happen with the guarantees from the federal Government on a number of loans, some of which could extend for as long as 15 years, in the event that those loans were not paid.
We are proposing to support the Minister's proposal of a six-month extension today in the hope and understanding that he will be able to convince his Cabinet colleagues that the only choice for the Farm Improvement Loans Act is that offered by the provincial Ministers of Agriculture and their Deputy Ministers, to strengthen the Farm Improvement Loans Act so that it can once again offer loans to farmers at fixed interest rates and for a term running from one to five years.
Let me explain the actual purpose of the Farm Improvement Loans Act. I have already indicated that it was established in 1945 to make it possible for farmers to obtain loans from banks for a medium term of one to five years. Later, it was expanded to permit loans for buildings and other assets which have a longer life so that a loan could run for as long as ten years. The possibility of buying land under the Farm Improvement Loans Act with loans running for as long as 15 years was
Farm Improvement Loans Act
included in the last two or three renewals of the legislation. The maximum loan currently offered is up to $100,000 with the interest rate set at the banks' prime rate plus 1 per cent. I think this is one of the things about which provincial Ministers and their deputies were concerned.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, under the last change to the Bank Act the kinds of loans which have become prevalent under Section 176 of the Bank Act are those where interest rates vary on a weekly basis and the borrower pays 1 per cent, 2 per cent or 3 per cent over that prime rate. The farmer does not really know what interest rate he will be paying six months from now or, indeed, even next week, because it changes.
Therefore, the provincial Ministers of Agriculture and their deputies suggested it was time to go back to a fixed rate for these kinds of loans in particular because farmers were being asked to pay rates considerably higher than inflation and considerably more than what agriculture could generate in terms of ability to repay. Since these loans are generally taken out by beginning farmers or those who are adding to their machinery and buildings, it is important the rate not be set too much higher than their ability to repay.
The terms of the loans are not unreasonable. They are very little different than what some of the banks will offer outside of the Farm Improvement Loans Act. A farmer must put up 25 per cent collateral on most loans with the loan amounting to up to 75 per cent of the value of the machinery, buildings or livestock. There has been one change with respect to the amount of assets the farmer or borrower must put up and that is when the purchaser wants to purchase real estate. In that case the loan can be for as much as 90 per cent of the value of the real estate.
The program has been designed to protect the lender-the banks, in most cases, although credit unions can also make loans under the Farm Improvement Loans Act-against losses. The federal Government provides some funding in the event there are losses. However, the losses have not been great under this program. Since 1945 the average losses claimed under this program have resulted in a cost to the federal Government under this Act in the amount of .2 per cent of 1 per cent, so we are talking about very small losses. In other words, farmers have been very good risks under this program and have used it very carefully.
Losses, however, have increased since the farm debt crisis which was triggered in 1981 by high interest rates. Losses in 1985 were expected to reach a high of about $5 million which, considering the total amount loaned and paid back, is still much less than 1 per cent of the total amount provided. Even at the increased rate of loss over the last few years, it is still far less than 1 per cent. It is not something about which the Nielsen task force had to worry. It is not a cost unduly high for the Government of Canada to carry. It costs something less than $5 million to keep the lending portfolios of the banks

December 15, 1986
Farm Improvement Loans Act
current as they effect loans under the Farm Improvement Loans Act.
I think it is important, if there is going to be a choice, and I want to reiterate this to the House, that the loans act continue in place, but not just for six months. We should go back to the three-year program which had been in place since 1945 and back to the fixed rate operation which made the program useful and usable up until recent times. Perhaps the House does not realize, but interest is becoming a very big part of farm costs. I would like to cite some figures and I know these are the kinds of things which put everyone to sleep. However, I think most everyone is asleep anyway, so what can I lose?
Pardon?

Between 1973 and 1975, as an example, farmers had $8.81 to $7.94 of net income for every dollar of interest they had to pay. Back in those days they had a fairly large amount of net income with which to make interest payments. Those were sort of the glory years for agriculture in terms of the farmers' ability to pay interest. Between 1979 and 1984 we went down hill badly. We went from $8.81 back in 1973 to $2.81 in 1984 of net income for every dollar of interest we had to pay, according to the latest figures. Within a decade we are left with a great deal of our net income going to the payment of interest rates.
It was a Liberal Government up to 1984, and then I believe it was a Conservative Government. I do not know what conclusion we should come to from that. On the surface one would have to say that with a Liberal Government in 1973 and the Conservative Government in 1984, things had gone down hill badly, but I think there was more to it than that.
I believe there is still a very great need for this kind of program. We have seen studies recently which show the need has become so great it has been recognized by the provinces who have been picking up on the fact that the Farm Improvement Loans program is not all it should be. Therefore, we have seen over past years a number of provincial programs which attempt to fill the need from which the federal Government appears to be backing away. Instead of the prime plus one kind of lending, we see provinces introducing programs which attempt to provide better, more stable financing for farmers, such as the Quebec Farm Improvement Loans Act which provides interest rates at prime plus one half of 1 per cent. That is only slightly better than the federal program, but it subsidizes the first 3 per cent of interest up to the first $15,000.
The program in British Columbia provides up to a maximum of $300,000. It is available to those people who are not eligible for credit under normal financing. The Province of Alberta has a similar kind of program but it has no maximum loan which can be made, therefore farmers can go over the $300,000 maximum which is available in British Columbia. The rest of the Alberta program is similar to the Farm Improvement Loans program.
The Province of Saskatchewan does not have a particular loan program except for some livestock operations. Its particular program provides interest rates at prime plus 2 per cent. It is aimed at those farmers who are having great difficulty in getting credit to expand their operations. Manitoba has a program which is limited to $60,000. That program is aimed at operating credit, as well as for some livestock and machinery. Ontario has an operating loan guarantee, but no intermediate loan guarantee, similar to the Farm Improvement Loans program, and the Atlantic region has no program at all.
I think it is useful to point out at this point in time that one of the reasons the Nielsen task force gave for getting rid of the farm improvement loans program was that most of the advantage ended up going to the cropping areas of the country, and in particular to Saskatchewan. The report was worded in such a way that it almost sounded as if it was the kind of program that could be very easily dropped since most of the advantage seemed to go to Saskatchewan. I do not know if the task force felt that Saskatchewan was not very important or if it simply felt that there was not very much political clout likely to come out of Saskatchewan which only has 14 Members of Parliament out of 282. At any rate, that assessment stands and the task force continues to stand by its proposal to do away with the program.
I think we should note just in passing that the Nielsen task force report said that its study team on business subsidies and services proposed the continuation with user-fees and reduced guarantees for the business improvement loans under the Small Businesses Loans Act. That loan activity is about three to four times the level of the Farm Improvement Loans Act and has 10 times the losses. The Nielsen task force thought that this program for small businesses should continue even though its loss ratio was much higher and it seems to be less effective than the Farm Improvement Loans Act. This discrepancy in the Nielsen task force was picked up on in part by the Ontario Institute of Agrologists which just completed a study that is in the hands of many Members of the House.
The Institute points out that in its opinion, the Nielsen task force has overrated some other aspects of the economy and underrated the importance of agriculture. It also points out that in one of his assessments of the Nielsen task force, Dean Freeman McEwen of the Ontario Agricultural College at Guelph was quoted in the press of October 27 of this year as saying:
He noted a task force led by former Deputy Prime Minister Erik Nielsen put farm subsidies and tax expenditures at $4.1 billion last year. He said small businesses received $16.4 billion in federal subsidies and services in 1985.
"I would be prepared to lay on the table side by side the contribution of agriculture to Canada and the contribution of small business to Canada," McEwen told a news conference in Aberfoyle near Guelph. "Small business is just getting a whale of a good deal."
Hon. Members who are generally aware of the importance of small business in the growth of Canada should also be aware that in the opinion of many experts who understand
December 15, 1986

agriculture better than those Hon. Members of Parliament, the contribution and potential contribution of agriculture to Canada far outweighs that of small business and that agicul-ture is not getting its fair share of assistance from this Government, nor did it get its fair share from previous Governments.
In closing, I would like to remind the House that using the floating rate loans which have been used for the last five or six years under the Farm Improvement Loans Act is in effect asking farmers to pay rates higher than the rate of inflation and much higher than the ability of farms to generate money to repay those loans. We are now asking farmers to pay in the neighbourhood of 11 per cent and 12 per cent for loans to add to the equipment, livestock and buildings on the farms and to add to their ability to produce. We are asking this at a time when inflation is somewhere between 4 per cent and 5 per cent. People who are lending money are therefore taking 6 per cent to 7 per cent of real interest.
When the Farm Improvement Loans Act program was begun the fixed rate was 5 per cent and inflation was between 2 and 3 per cent. Real interests was 2 per cent to 3 per cent at most. For the last nearly 10 years, we have been asked to carry high real interest rates when agriculture as an entity across Canada has only rarely been able to generate profits in excess of 2 per cent or 3 per cent. The ability to repay stands at 2 per cent or 3 per cent, but the cost agriculture is being asked to bear stands at 6 per cent or 7 per cent in real interest rates terms. This makes it virtually impossible for young, albeit, efficient farmers to carry these rates.
In the last few seconds that I shall speak on this issue today I would like to make a renewed call to all government Members. I realize the Minister has probably had this matter before Cabinet for some time. I would hope that when Cabinet must make a final decision on supporting the Farm Improvement Loans Act at fixed rates as Agriculture Ministers across Canada have proposed, the Government will listen to those Agriculture Ministers and will ignore the inappropriate and inopportune recommendation of the Nielsen task force so that we may continue to make this program available to farmers in the future.

speechtext:
Order. House in Committee of the Whole on Bill C-31, an Act to amend the Farm Improvement Loans Act.
Shall Clause 1 carry?
On Clause 1-

Mr. Chairman, I have a few questions for the Minister on the Farm Improvement Loans Act. Has the program been subscribed to the maximum level of the funds that are available? Why have a program like this which is so sparsely utilized in provinces like Ontario, for instance? The program seems to be well used in Saskatchewan and the other prairie provinces, but it is not utilized to any great extent in Ontario. Is it simply the case that all the available loan guarantees are totally used up, or is it the case of the banks simply refusing to issue loans under this program because they can make more money issuing loans under some other program? Would the Government be willing to require that a certain level of its funding be made available under this program?
Even today many farmers are stuck with borrowing funds at 12 and 15 per cent. Obviously, the industry cannot afford this. For instance, only 9.5 per cent of the funds are used in Ontario, which is the second largest agricultural producing province, and it may have as large a capacity as Saskatchewan. Why is this program gradually running down? In 1979 there were 25,000 loans made available. In 1984 there were only 12,000 loans made available, even though the interest rate advantage is desperately needed today, perhaps even more so than in 1979. Could the Minister inform the House about those matters?

Saskatchwan has the greatest participation rate with 38 per cent utilization. The second province is Alberta with 29.3 per cent. The third is Manitoba with 12.8 per cent. The fourth is Ontario with 9.5 per cent. The fifth is British Columbia with 4.1 per cent.
The Hon. Member's question is interesting and one to which we have been attempting to seek the answer. The provincial industry rate subsidy programs are not as enticing and beneficial as, for example, those of the provinces of Quebec or Nova Scotia. I stand to be corrected, but I believe that the Province of Prince Edward Island also has a fairly good provincial program and interest rate reduction, and perhaps there might be some other programs. First, I am tempted to believe that it is the nature of farmers because the program is a national program; second, the banks carry out the same program and apply the same policy across the country. We have been asking staff people who have been associated with this program for longer than you and I, Mr. Chairman, and that is also the question that we are putting to farm organizations. There does not seem to be a legitimate reason for it.

Farm Improvement Loans Act
With respect to the other question that the Hon. Member raises, it sounds to me as if he has been reading some of my old speeches when I was in Opposition. I can recall that during those days the bankers used to have three stock answers: One, they had never heard of the program before; it was not their policy to lend under the Farm Improvement Loans Act; that their allotment or quota was totally used up. Of course, we know it is nonsense, all three observations.
There has been some discussion that perhaps to provide a greater incentive for the banks to participate to a greater extent we may have to consider a slight increase over prime plus one, that is, if we wish greater participation in the program. That does not interest me very much, and I am sure it does not interest the farm community or the farm leadership.
These are some of the hard questions in respect of which we need time to sit down with more farm organizations, to determine exactly in which direction they would prefer us to go.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: On a supplementary question, the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster).

I am interested in knowing whether the Minister is personally committed to the idea of requiring that a certain percentage of the loans made to farmers by the chartered banks, whether they would have to be made available under the Farm Improvement Loans Act when the Government is reviewing it during the next six months. Is the Government giving consideration to extending this to cover working capital as well as capital items such as machinery, land, and improvements? Is the Government prepared to consider that in its plan?
I ask these things, Mr. Chairman, because the current rate of interest, the real interest that many farmers are paying, is almost as high today as it was in 1981 or 1982 during the high rates of interest. The inflation rate back in those days was 10 or 11 per cent. If interest rates were 17 or 18 per cent in those days, and today they are 10 or 12 per cent with inflation rates that are only 3 or 4 per cent, the interest rate is still high. That is why there has been the tremendous downturn in farm asset value. For instance, the Farm Credit Corporation told the Standing Committee on Agriculture last week that farm asset values had dropped by almost 7 per cent in the last 12 months. That means that if the farm asset values were $100 billion in the summer or fall of 1985, they were some $7 billion less, or almost double the net farm income. With this tremendous drop in farm asset values, it is little wonder that so many farmers who are heavily leveraged are losing their equity and facing the loss of their land because their equity is going down. Any move toward giving lower interest rates will benefit that situation. Certainly, many farmers complain about paying 12, 13, or 14 per cent even though theoretically there is money available under this program at 1 per cent above prime. Could the Minister give us some indication on this points?

I have listened to the Hon. Member's speech and had some difficulty following the logic of it. His first question seemed to be quite sensible and reasonable, but I had the feeling that he is slipping back into that questionable logic that he expressed in his speech.
One of the major contributing factors and why we are dealing with a very serious financial difficulty in agriculture today is a direct result of the lack of programs, action, commitment, and financial support provided to the farm community over that period of time when the Hon. Member was a government Member. What were some of the messages flowing out of that Government that he was a member of? Well, they indicated that the inflation rate would remain constant throughout this period of time that we are presently going through. Of course, that turned out to be dead wrong.
The second observation was that the commodity prices would be at an all time high. Of course, we see them at an all time low for the last 50-year period. The Hon. Member's Government indicated that energy costs would remain constant throughout this period of time. It did not foresee what would happen to energy costs. It indicated that we would be going through a period of time when we would experience a shortage of commodities. All major food producing countries in the world are going through a period of surplus in supply, so they were dead wrong. They also indicated that interest rates would remain stable throughout the latter part of the 1970s and throughout the 1980s. However, what happened to interest rates? They went from 9 per cent to 24 per cent.
We have talked with young farmers across the country, day in and day out, seven days a week. We asked them what was a major contributing factor to the financial difficulties they were experiencing. They say that it was interest rates. They planned their operations on 9 per cent and 10 per cent interest rates, but interest rates increased from 9 per cent to 24 per cent. That is what killed them; that is what crippled them.
Every 1 per cent of interest rate is a cost to Canadian farmers of about $140 million. Interest rates increased from 9 per cent to 24 per cent or some 15 points. All one has to do is a mathematical calculation to arrive at the result to the farm community.
When the Liberal Government was in office it transferred an added input cost to Canadian farmers of about $2 billion. What did they do about it? We cannot say they did nothing, because they had a little program called the Special Farm Assistance Program. It was selective, and it helped about 1,900 farmers. However, who paid for it? It was not the Consolidated Revenue Fund. It was fellow borrowers, fellow clients of the Farm Credit Corporation, who paid. We changed that. We took that extra burden off the shoulders of FCC clients and we picked it up, thanks to the support of my colleagues and the Minister of Finance. We are picking up the extra $80 million, affecting some 5,600 clients.
December 15, 1986

I understand the frustration of the Hon. Member who was a government Member for a long time. He campaigned and provided election commitments to farmers. He came back here and sat in the Liberal Government benches, and that Government did not fulfil any of the campaign commitments. I understand his frustration. When he compares the record of his Government to the record of this Government, I understand his frustration.

Mr. Chairman, the only clause with which we are dealing today provides that during the period from July 1, 1980 through to June 30, 1987, $1,550 million will be made available to the banks for guarantees on loans during that period of time. Could the Minister update us on how much of that allocation has already been used? Is the extension over the seven years an increase, a decrease, or a continuation of the same level of loan guarantees to banking institutions?

Mr. Chairman, I have checked with my officials and they indicate that we have at least a half billion dollars to be utilized. If the past is any indication of what future requirements might be, and no doubt it will be, there would be an adequate amount of money left to deal with the demand on the Farm Improvement Loans Act.

Mr. Chairman, in the report of the Nielsen task force, the subcommittee looking at farm credit and the Farm Improvement Loans Act, it was indicated that losses were still less than 1 per cent. In other words, the guarantees the Government was required to make to the end of 1984 were still below 1 per cent. Could we have an update on what percentage of losses we are facing in more recent times?
Mr. Chairman, we would have in the portfolio about $5 billion. Our losses would be $4.8 million. I gather that would be less than 1 per cent.

Mr. Chairman, I will make a slight change in direction. In one of the Minister's responses to the Hon. Member for Algoma he speculated that perhaps it might be necessary to extend the interest rate from 1 per cent to 1.5 per cent or 2 per cent of prime. I want to raise that issue with him because it seemed to be somewhat of a psychological slip.
I understood that we would try to go to a fixed rate rather than to an increase in the floating rate. Is it an indication that the Minister is beginning to waver and listen to some of his cabinet colleagues? Will we be looking at a fixed rate? At what range of interest is he looking for the fixed rate? Will it be just a few percentage points over the real interest rate or the rate of inflation?

No, Mr. Chairman. I want to make very clear that it was not a slip of the tongue or anything of that nature. It was a frank observation of one of the options we might consider. There is no way in legislation to force the banks to participate to any extent or to increase their participation to a greater extent under the program. It would be nothing short of wishful thinking.
Farm Improvement Loans Act
If it is the conclusion of farm leaders that they want greater participation in the loan program, and obviously that would be one way in which we could successfully encourage the banks to participate to a greater extent. I think it is just a reality. We may have to consider it as one of the options.
I indicated that it was not good news to me-and I am sure it would not be good news to Canadian farmers-because farmers would like to see greater participation at the existing prime plus one or perhaps prime plus a half like they have in Quebec. I do not know, but we will have to look at it. I made that observation deliberately.
I listened to the Hon. Member's speech when he talked about a 41 year history. I do not know what period of time it was; I have not had a chance to check it. However, he indicated that there were fixed rates over that period. It is an option which we will have to consider. I think it would be an option which farmers perhaps would support. No doubt they would be prepared to pay a bit of a premium for that stability in the program.
Farm leaders have suggested other options. One was that perhaps we could raise the $100,000 limit. Maybe we should consider other criteria to be eligible. At the moment quotas and things of that nature are not eligible under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. I do not know what we would do on that one. It would depend upon the position taken by farm leaders. I see the Hon. Member smiling. He knows the problem there as well as I do.
Also, an individual can have one, two, three, four, or more farm improvement loans. Perhaps for administrative purposes it would be possible for him to put them all under one loan. There are a number of things at which we could look, but certainly fixed interest would be helpful.

Mr. Chairman, in one of my other lives I am a member of the Standing Committee on Public Accounts. Every time we ask Government Members and Deputy Ministers why they have done certain things they tell us that this is part of the restraint emanating from the Nielsen task force or the task force which attempted to review it. Many of us got the impression that the task force report was put on the shelf and ignored. Obviously it was put on the shelf as far as Parliament was concerned, but not as far as the departments are concerned.
Because of the different approach that the Nielsen task force took on this legislation, can the Minister assure us-I am pleased to hear the Minister talking about certain changes that might be plausible-that one of those changes is not a recommendation of the Nielsen task force which was to eliminate this Act and program entirely six months down the road? I know the Minister has been talking around this suggestion quite a bit this morning. I still want that assurance that we are not talking about a six months extension and then the elimination of the program.

December 15, 1986
Farm Improvement Loans Act

Mr. Chairman, the Hon. Member poses two questions. He talks about restraint. This is Government restraint and it has to be by necessity. To continue to spend money like our predecessors we would be taking $3 out of every $4 of taxpayers' money simply to carry the interest on the debt. We would not have any money for small business people, for farmers, for grains and oil seeds people, and who knows who else would fall in line. If the Hon. Member examines the record, restraint on behalf of our Government has not reached Canadian farmers.
If we compare our contribution to our predecessors, we are up $2.7 billion this year, not counting the latest billion. Since we have assumed office, our Government has taken 350 initiatives delivering $5.7 billion directly into the pockets of Canadian farmers. Again, that does not include the latest billion which would bring the total to $6.7 billion. Because of the importance of agriculture domestically and internationally, and because of the priority the Government places on agriculture-yes, Canadian farmers are going through difficult times, the most difficult in 50 years-we are responding to those difficulties to the maximum of our financial capabilities.
Hon. Members always seem to misunderstand the Nielsen task force. Maybe they do so for their own purposes from time to time. I suggest that perhaps it might be, but we must remember that the Nielsen task force expressed options and recommendations. These options and recommendations are not Government policy. I repeat and I am sure I will have to say it again, they are not Government policy. If we had followed the recommendation in the Nielsen task force we would not have delivered to the dairy farmers the long term dairy policy of $1.5 billion; we would not have doubled the advance payments crop legislation, and I do not think that we would have extended this Act. I do not know which preceded which, the last extension or the tabling of the Nielsen task force. The only appropriate message that I can send to the Hon. Member, which should give him some comfort, is that if it were Government policy to let the program expire, then we would not be here today asking for a six month extension. We are asking for a little more time to consult with the farm leaders. We could have acted unilaterally. We could have been back here with a three year extension right now. That is not what we prefer to do. We want to take the necessary time to carry out consultations with the farm community to ensure greater utilization of this Act.

I would point out just as a comment, Mr. Chairman, that there are a number of recommendations about agriculture in the Nielsen task force that have been put into effect, restraints are taking place and there are increases in charges in a number of areas and so on. The suggestion that agriculture is outside of the task force report and that other areas are not using the recommendations does not follow through.

Mr. Speaker, I, too, would like to express my gratitude to the Opposition Parties and their official critics for allowing us to expedite Bill C-32 which was introduced and given first reading earlier this day.
The history of the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act is slightly different than that of the Farm Improvement Loans Act, it having been first adopted in December, 1955. However, the purpose of this Act is much the same as that of the Farm Improvement Loans Act which was just debated in this Chamber. Loans guaranteed under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act are guaranteed to a specified ceiling within a designated period.
The present period, Period 9, as provided for in Section 6(2) of the legislation, will expire December 31, 1986, unless the
amendment the Government is proposing today is approved by all Parties. This Bill will do nothing more than alter the date appearing on page 108-9 in Section 6(1) of the present Fisheries Improvement Loans Act which says that the payments to lenders are guaranteed up to December 31, 1986.
Since its inception in December of 1955 the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act has guaranteed some 18,000 loans totaling $246 million, most of which have been repaid without claims under the provisions of this Act. As at the end of the last fiscal year there was approximately $13.5 million in claims against total loans of $246 million for a default rate of about 5.5 per cent, which is not at all alarming.
The Bill is designed to facilitate credit to fishermen who need money for the purchase or construction of a fishing vessel, the purchase or construction of equipment such as auxiliary boats, engines, winches, electronic equipment, nets and so forth, or for the major repair or overhaul of a fishing vessel.
The legislation presently in place authorizes the federal Government to guarantee lenders against losses incurred on loans made in accordance with its provisions. It specifies that the maximum amount which a fisherman may have outstanding under the provisions of the Act at any one time may not exceed $150,000 and the maximum repayment period is 15 years. The rate of interest charged on loans guaranteed under the Act is set at 1 per cent over the prime lending rate of chartered banks. This is a very favourable rate for fishermen with the present level being 10.75 plus 1 per cent. The rate under the legislation floats with the prime rate for the duration of the loan.
The legislation also sets out the total principal amount of guaranteed loans that may be made by all lending institutions lending funds under this Act during the lending period. The present approved level for Period 9, which would have expired on December 31 of this year, is $30 million. There is a portion of that $30 million which has not yet been secured by borrowers which allows us to propose, by way of this amendment, a six-month extension of the provisions of the Act.
Loans granted under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act must be secured in the form of a chattel or marine mortgage on the item purchased or constructed and the lender is given a written promise by the borrower to repay the loan. It should be noted that if the borrower defaults he or she remains liable to the Crown for the repayment of that loan when the lending institution is compensated under this Act. Other terms and conditions of each loan are worked out between the applicant and the lender.
We are asking for a six-month extension to the present Period 9 of loan authority in order to consider options to improve our program of providing financial services and assistance to fishermen. For example, the loans extended during Periods 6 and 7 from 1977 to 1982 have resulted in a rate of default considerably in excess of the ceilings provided for within the Act. This has caused problems for many
December 15, 1986

fishermen. In addition, we are looking for means to integrate more effectively our loan support assistance with the programs provided by provincial loans boards. As well, we are looking at options for financing fishermen through the Federal Business Development Bank, for instance, or by way of a meshing of this program with the Small Businesses Loans Act. For all of these reasons we have asked for a six-month extension with a view to improving financial services and access to loans on the part of fishermen. We will require no additional financial support to facilitate this extension.
Therefore, I am asking the co-operation of all Members of the House in ensuring that this amendment is given speedy passage today. It is important to maintain continuity in the provision of loans to fishermen through to the proposed termination date of June 30, 1987. I invite response from members of the Opposition at this committee stage and I hope we can pass the legislation in a timely way.

Mr. Chairman, I want to speak briefly to the amendment to the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. The Minister is correct that this Bill extends the effect of the Act for an additional six months and I am pleased with the reasons he has given for doing so. It is a good program which I believe the Minister should have extended for a year or longer. However, there are certain problems with it, such as the 10 per cent ceiling with respect to banks. I am also pleased that the Minister will use this six-month extension to consider options for improving the legislation.
The Nielsen Task Force report presented options to the House some time ago, including a recommendation that the Government consider termination of the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, since less federal Government intervention in fisheries and allowing the industry to function in response to market forces are major thrusts of the study. Such was the conclusion of the study team which went on to say, to that extent, that financial assistance required by fishermen can be obtained from provincial loan boards or financial institutions. I hope this is not happening to this program and that the Minister is serious when he says the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act will continue and be improved to meet the needs of those for whom it is designed so that fishermen can meet their obligations in the industry.
I am somewhat skeptical because many other good fisheries programs have been phased out by the Government in the past. For example, there is the vessel subsidy program that was very important to fishermen and enabled them to obtain a one-third subsidy from the federal Government and assist them in obtaining loans from financial institutions.

subtopic: FARM DEBT REVIEW ACT-CRITICISM OF LEGISLATION
FARM DEBT REVIEW ACT-CRITICISM OF LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last June when the House debated and passed the Farm Debt Review Act, my colleagues and I expressed grave concerns that the Act would be ineffective. We said that the Act provided no real incentives to creditors to be reasonable in adjusting terms of credit to farmers. In short, we said that the Act had no teeth.
We have been proven right. Farmers are telling us that the review system is not working. Not only are the boards heavily overworked but too many creditors simply are not interested in finding workable solutions to the problems.
Even the good friend of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise), Premier Devine, is unimpressed with the Farm Debt Review Act. The Premier has said that the federal Act is so inadequate that his Government has been forced to extend the Saskatchewan Farmland Security Act. At least the Saskatchewan Act allows farmers to appeal to the court if a creditor proves to be unreasonable. I therefore call upon the Minister of Agriculture to prepare amendments to strengthen the federal Farm Debt Review Act which will undergo a statutory review early in the new year.

ESCALATION OF VIOLENCE IN INDIAN SUB-CONTINENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, violence of an ethnic or religious origin appears to be escalating in the Indian sub-continent. To illustrate, let us take three headlines from this morning's Globe and Mail'. "54 killed, 310
injured in Pakistani ethnic riot", "Hindus riot in Amritsar after funeral of politician", and "25 Tamils left dead in clashes".
What greater affront to human rights can there be than when people are wantonly murdered and forced to live in fear for their very lives? Canada has always spoken out on human rights violations and ought to use all its persuasive powers through the United Nations, the Commonwealth, and its relations with the countries involved to bring about a reduction in these unnecessary killings.

Mr. Speaker, I have in my hand a copy of the restricted memo which has just come from the Canadian Armed Forces regarding the charter task force report. After extensive study which involved no discussion with anyone outside of the Armed Forces, the task force concluded that there is currently insufficient positive evidence that mixed gender employment could be further expanded without an adverse impact on operational effectiveness.
Since when is it the responsibility of the citizens of Canada to prove equality? In fact the specific instructions given to the Armed Forces by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Beatty) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) were to find ways of implementing equality. After extensive examination which involved no outside discussion whatsoever, the armed forces have concluded that they cannot promote equality today but two years hence they might be prepared to do so. I say that that particular guarantee is not enough. I would ask the Minister of National Defence to step in immediately and determine that a task force on operational effectiveness includes civilians as well as members of the military, so that we can ensure true equality for minorities in this country.

subtopic: IMPOSITION OF FOOD PRICE INCREASES ON ZAMBIAN PEOPLE
IMPOSITION OF FOOD PRICE INCREASES ON ZAMBIAN PEOPLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the International Monetary Fund could learn a lesson from recent events in Zambia where looting and rioting took place following the abolition of food subsidies. At the urging of the IMF, the Government had doubled the price of corn meal, which is the staple diet of urban Zambians. The situation became so bad that President Kaunda had to restore food subsidies.
The IMF must stop imposing economic prescriptions which disregard social realities and widespread poverty in less developed countries. The gap in outlook between the IMF boardroom and the conditions of people in the streets of Lusaka is alarming. Forcing the doubling of the price of corn meal can have devastating repercussions on people whose pockets are virtually empty.
The IMF must come to its senses, recognize the importance of non-monetary values, and replace its insensitive policy with one that recognizes the social reality that the North must accept, namely, the debt situation of the least developed countries cannot be corrected by forcing Governments directly or indirectly to increase the price of food or the level of unemployment.
