AWARDING OF CONTRACT FOR PORT-CARTIER PRISON-POSSIBLE CONFLICT OF INTEREST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is also directed to the Prime Minister and concerns the awarding of a contract at Port-Cartier. This morning, the President of the Treasury Board informed the House that Bechtel was awarded a contract because its proposal was judged to be the best, and I am quoting directly. Is it not a fact that this proposal was the best one because it was the only one that would fit the Prime Minister's political agenda? And why did the Government fail to follow the guidelines of the conflict of interest legislation, the provisions
of Section 49 that make it quite clear the contract should never have been awarded to Bechtel?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
subtopic: AWARDING OF CONTRACT FOR PORT-CARTIER PRISON-POSSIBLE CONFLICT OF INTEREST
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the conflict of interest guidelines were followed in this case. After a detailed investigation of all the facts, I announced this morning that the Government wanted to rescind the contract awarded to Bechtel because there was both an apparent and a real conflict of interest in this case.

Mr. Speaker, offering a few heads did not work for Ronald Reagan, and it is not going to work today here either.
My supplementary question for the Prime Minister concerns the statement that Correctional Services and Public Works will now be continuing to direct the Port-Cartier project. Can the Prime Minister tell us how it is that the Member for Halifax, the former Minister of Supply and Services, could not administer the contract in that role and that he has now been given the responsibility for administering similar or the same contracts in his new role of Minister of Public Works? Should he not be fired instead of being given new contracts to administer? Is it not obvious that he cannot do that job?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the procedure that we are following is very normal. It is the typical procedure for any government.
Typical Tory.

It is normal for any government, Mr. Speaker. We have decided to rescind the contract to Bechtel for the reasons I outlined this morning, and the responsible Departments which are Public Works, the Department of Supply and Services, and Correctional Services, will ensure that the work is continued and a new contract is awarded.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister decided to rescind the contract only after the Government was caught doing something it ought never to have done in the first place.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. There were two statements this morning, one by the Auditor General and one by the Minister. The Auditor General said, his words, not mine, that the Government showed preferential treatment in making this decision. In his statement in the House afterwards, the Minister, incredibly, blamed everyone, including civil servants, but the Government itself. He said the reason all these normal contractual procedures were broken was because the decision had been reached to build the prison within "a tight schedule". Will the Prime Minister now acknowledge the
December 15, 1986

reason this schedule was imposed is that he decided to give himself a gift in his own riding for political purposes?

Mr. Speaker, the statement by my hon. friend is absolutely inaccurate. There was no such indication by me or my office at any time in any circumstances. If my hon. friend wishes to be fair in his analysis, the completion date was imposed by the previous Government with regard to a substitute facility for Laval. I do not change at all nor do I make any apologies for the Government decision to locate it in Port-Cartier pursuant to criteria set out by the former Solicitor General in the Liberal Government.
We took a decision concerning Port-Cartier and we stand by that decision. It was a proper and honourable decision for a region of this country which is entitled to some assistance and should never be penalized simply because it is represented by a Prime Minister, or another Minister, or the Leader of the NDP.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister knows perfectly well that the decision made by the previous Government concerned a prison in another community, not a community in the Prime Minister's riding. That is a fact.
My question to the Prime Minister is simply this: Why is the Government blaming everyone, even its officials, for the Government's decision to build a penitentiary in the Prime Minister's riding for purely political reasons?

Mr. Speaker, that too is entirely false. The Government is not blaming anyone. The President of the Treasury Board quite appropriately initiated an investigation, and he has drawn a number of conclusions from that investigation to date.
You were referring to another prison, in a riding in New Brunswick, and comparing it with the riding of Manicouagan. I hope the Leader of the New Democratic Party is not claiming that peripheral areas like the North Shore and Eastern Quebec do not have a right to federal facilities, because I can tell you that federal Government facilities in remote areas are very rare indeed. In my own riding there were none.
That was why the Government decided it was entirely fair and honourable to act in the interests of efficiency. We could build all federal facilities between Ottawa and Toronto, but that would be unfair to the rest of the country.

Mr. Speaker, we do not need to listen to lectures about regional development. We
Oral Questions
believe there ought to be regional development in all the poorer parts of this country, including the Prime Minister's riding.
Hear, hear!
However, we do not believe in squandering $41 million of the public's money for electoral reasons. That is the difference.
Hear, hear!

If the Prime Minister would like to put an end to this and get it out of the House of Commons, will he get up and acknowledge that this decision was a mistake, taken at the highest level of government, and the Government will now commit itself to integrity in government and put an end to short run political decisions?
My hon. friend says he is in favour of regional economic development, including the constituency of Manicouagan.
Yes.

Then perhaps he could tell us what he has in mind for Port-Cartier? During the time in question a substantial part of the population was out of work without any hope at all, and without any help from the federal Government. In fact, if you examine the record of the federal Government with regard to development in the constituency of Manicouagan, in the interior of British Columbia, or in northern Ontario, you will find that it was very, very wanting.
The present Government believes in fairness. We make no apologies to anyone for making decisions which result in no squandering of public funds. I can think of no better use of public funds than for the Government of Canada to signal to people in faraway regions that taxpayers' money will be spent on them and their children for the future so they will not have to seek exile elsewhere in Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. House in Committee of the Whole on Bill C-32, an Act to amend the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. When the committee was interrupted at 1.25
December 15, 1986

o'clock p.m., Clause 1 of the Bill was under consideration and the Hon. Member for Egmont had the floor.

Mr. Chairman, when the Chair called it 1.25 I was mentioning that the Government and the Ministers are not making as a priority the fishing industry of Canada. At that time I cited some of the programs of the previous Government that were extremely beneficial to the fishing industry but were eliminated by this Government. Of course, this ties in with the Bill we are discussing here today because it does relate specifically to the income of fishermen.
When I talked about the vessel subsidy program, I related how helpful it was for fishermen who made large capital expenditures on their vessels and equipment. These fishermen could use the one-third vessel subsidy allotted to them by the federal Government as part of a down payment or collateral required to obtain a vessel or upgrade one.
I would also like to mention the insignificant amount of funds the Government is giving to small craft harbours. Only approximately $46 million will be going into small craft harbours this year. Every Hon. Member who comes from a fishing community will realize that that is a mere pittance compared to what is needed for a very worth-while industry.
I receive letters daily from people from all over Canada. I have a copy of a letter addressed to the Minister that I wish to read into Hansard. It reads:
Dear Mr. Minister
I wish to draw to your attention the deplorable state of affairs.
The wharfage situation in Comox-Courtenay area is inadequate to say the least. The overcrowding and potential fire hazard on the present site is a deterrent to anyone having a vessel on these premises.
One has to wonder if this riding being N.D.P. has any connection with your apathy towards investing in the Comox Valley wharfage facilities.
Your past performance indicates you run to the pork-barrel to grease the skids of your constituency-Tom; prove me wrong.
This letter is from the West Coast. I have received a hundred letters from people there who are complaining to me that they are in dire need of a better infrastructure as it relates to their wharfs, harbours and piers.
Of course, it is the same thing on the Atlantic coast. Almost every harbour wharf needs some work done. The amount of money this Government is putting into these programs has a direct relationship to the income of fishermen. In order to get the best price for the product they take from the waters, fishermen have to have good quality, ice on board, unloading derricks, and a fast mode of transportation to get their product to the processing plant and to the consumer as quickly as possible. These are some of the areas in which this Government and this Minister have let the fishing industry of this country down, and let it down badly.
On top of that, there is the imposition of user fees, the doubling of licencing fees on the West Coast, and there are many other aspects to the fishing industry that are not at all
Fisheries Improvement Loans Act
being dealt with to the satisfaction of the fishermen and the industry. I must emphasize that this is a very important industry. On the Atlantic coast, it is one of our largest industries. Thousands of families depend solely on the fishery. Any lessening of effort by the federal Government toward the well-being of the fishery is certainly not accepted in good light in Altantic Canada.
We are going to give consent to this extension for six months. I will take the Minister at his word, but I will ask the question later on, does the Minister mean what he says, that he is going to bring the Bill back in six months time with improvements? There are some flaws in the Bill, and were they corrected they would certainly go a long way to helping the fishermen who are in dire straits. There are many areas in Atlantic Canada that had a very poor fishing season this year. Along with the other program cuts, there is the Forget Commission Report which comes down very hard on the side of fishermen. There is a lot of concern right now in the industry about what this Government is doing on their behalf. I will end with these few remarks, Mr. Chairman. I am sure I have some colleagues who wish to follow me, and I may have some questions later on.

I am glad to have the opportunity to make a few remarks with regard to Bill C-32, amendments to the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act which will extend the life of that Act for another six months. In the New Democratic Party we are quite happy to give agreement to quick passage of this Bill, because this is obviously an Act that has provided a program of some help to some individuals in the fishing industry. For example, in the last year for which we have a report, 1984-85, there were 879 loans guaranteed which totalled almost $15 million. Since the program's inception in 1955 to the year 1984-85 there were 17,253 loans totalling some $227 million. Over the life of the program some $10 million was paid out in claims to lending agencies for loans that were in difficulty. It is important to recognize that $8.5 million of that $10 million was paid out in the last four years of the program, during which the fishing industry was having difficult times when it was caught in a squeeze between high input costs and very poor returns.
While the program may be good for some individuals, we have no idea what the Government thinks about the program's effect over the long term on the industry as whole. The Government does not know. That is why we are dealing with a six-month extension at the present time. That is why in June of 1985 the Government came before the House for an 18-month extension. At that time the then Minister said, as recorded at page 6161 of Hansard for June 15, 1985:
In the event that any Members wonder why that is so-
He was referring to why they were asking for an 18-month extension.
-it is of course because all programs including this one are being carefully reviewed. In the meantime, I think it is in the interests of the fishing community that speedy passage of this Bill be given by the House.

December 15, 1986
Fisheries Improvement Loans Act
The program review to which the then Minister referred was tabled in the House on March 11. It was available to the Government before that time, but it still has not indicated what its plans are for the fishing industry.
With regard to this particular program, the Nielsen committee task force stated:
A major problem in the fisheries, which has been identified by many studies, is over-capacity with too many fishermen pursuing too few fish. This program can be seen as adding to this problem, and is inconsistent with federal programs to buy back fishing licences to reduce efforts in the industry.
The effect of this program is to subsidize low-risk fishermen who would be able to obtain credit through normal channels, as well as high-risk fishermen who are required to put up little of their own money.
It is not quite that easy even for low-risk fishermen to get loans through normal channels. The banks want some guarantee. The task force further states:
The study team recommends to the Task Force that the Government consider termination of the Fisheries Improvement Loans Program. A major thrust of the study team's recommendations is for less federal Government intervention in the fisheries, and for allowing the industry to function in response to true market forces.
We have seen in the last few months a move by the Government to quietly implement some of the recommendations the Nielsen task force has made; to implement these without adequate debate, either in the House or within the fishing industry itself. Fishing licences have doubled. There have been cuts in the Department of Fisheries and Oceans staff. There have been cuts in research. There have been cuts in the Fishing Vessel Assistance Program. All these things have been done on an ad hoc basis without giving either the House or the industry any idea of what the Government's over-all plan or policy is.
There are two theories as to what the Government is doing here. I and my colleagues in caucus have a disagreement on this. There are those of us who feel that what the Government is doing is a matter of piecemeal adhockery; that it does not know itself what it is trying to do and what its objectives are, but it is doing it anyhow. The other theory is that there is a conspiracy that the Government really does know what it is doing, and even when it stumbles and falls it is stumbling and falling towards some objective. I subscribe to the First theory, that the Government does not know what it is doing. Whatever the explanation, there is a great deal of uncertainty in the industry. That should be of concern to Members on all sides of the House.
One subject that has already been referred to is the unemployment insurance program as it relates to people in the fishing industry. The Nielsen task force report, as well as the recently tabled Forget Commission report, recommends doing away with unemployment insurance for people who are in the fishing industry. The Forget Commission Report recommends that it should be phased out over a five-year program. The Government has refused to indicate that it categorically rejects that type of recommendation which would be extremely harmful to fishing communities and fishing provinces on both coasts of Canada. It has not categorically rejected that. Instead it says that it will take the Forget Commission report
as a background paper, a $5.2 million background paper, and will tell us its plans next May.
During the election campaign Conservative Members on the West Coast promised that there would be a $100 million buyback program to reduce the capacity of the fleet. We have not heard anything about it in the last few months. There is no buy-back program. Fishermen are being squeezed out despite the good season.
There is a story in the current issue of the union paper, The Fisherman, about a West Coast fisherman who is quitting after 30 years. Even though there was a good season on the coast, he lost money. He talks about the short openings, a recurrent feature of fisheries management today, and indicates there is almost panic among fishermen to get out there and get fish regardless of the weather. Some 16 fishermen lost their lives on the West Coast in the last year. He points to a fear that the time of the small independent fisherman might be almost over, and that if the industry survives, it will survive in the form of fish farms or aquaculture or through a centralized fleet in the hands of a few large companies.
While the six month extension of the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act might help some individuals, my concern is that it will not solve the basic problem of uncertainty. There is a need for the Government to eliminate uncertainty by indicating a clear process of consultation, so that those most involved in the industry can help determine their own future. The Government has done away with the MAC, the Minister's advisory committee, and has established a system wherein a committee will be appointed by the Minister himself. However, there is considerable skepticism on the coast about whether or not it will work.
I suggest to the Minister and to the Government as a whole that there should be no more expensive decoys such as the Nielsen task force report or the Forget Commission report. The Government should come clean with what it hopes to do and establish a process which will allow the people most involved in the industry to have a say in it.
Bill C-32 will mean that one piece of the jigsaw, the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, will be in place for the next six months. However, the rest of the jigsaw is scattered all over; people have no idea what will be the over-all pattern. The Minister indicated that changes were needed to resolve the problem involved in the limitation of guarantees once a certain level of claim for debts and difficulties has been reached. The difficulty was pointed out to the Minister in the last few months. At the very time when conditions were most difficult for fishermen, they found that their loans were being called by the banks because the guarantees had become inoperative. The Minister is aware of the problem. He has promised to do something about it by next spring. We look forward to the changes which he promised to bring in.
December 15, 1986

I should like to draw a final item to the attention of the Minister. Recently he won a court case in which his power to allocate between gear types and socio-economic conditions was deemed to be within his jurisdiction under the Constitution. Bill C-32 which gives him these powers is no longer necessary and, as the sunset clause becomes operative, it will die. However, Bill C-32 also guarantees consultation with the industry. I suggest that the Minister should reintroduce legislation in the House to reinstate the guarantee of consultation with the industry so that the people most affected will have the knowledge that the consultation is being written into the law, that it is not something just at the whim of the Minister.
In conclusion, we are glad to give support to the six month extension, but we urge the Government to come in with a process which will remove uncertainty in the fishing industry on both coasts, so that the fishing communities and the people involved in the industry will have some idea of what the future holds for them.

Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to participate in the debate on Bill C-32. I should like to echo the words of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Egmont, the critic for the Liberal Party. We in the Liberal Party are prepared to see the Bill receive rather speedy approval today, but we have some problem with it.
The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans has been aware for the last year of the great numbers of fishermen across Canada who through no fault of their own have defaulted on guaranteed fisheries improvement loans. They defaulted particularly last year, more so than this year, because of the nature of the fisheries and of the economy associated with it. They were rather amazed, indeed shocked, to discover that their so-called guaranteed federal fisheries improvement loans were not guaranteed at all. Fishermen have discovered that because of the fine print in the Bill, which we are now extending for six months, the Minister can say at his discretion when a particular lending institution has reached its quota of bad loans.
For example, if 10 per cent of the loans of the Bank of Nova Scotia in a lending zone and during a lending period-and that is the terminology used-turn out to be bad loans and it makes a claim on the Government of Canada, any other fisherman who defaults, unlike his neighbours and colleagues, does not have the benefit of the Government of Canada guaranteeing his bad loan. Fishermen have found out that lending institutions will come after them with collection agencies or people making third party demands.
I wrote a letter to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans in which I illustrated one particular case a year ago. In fact, in October, 1985 I made initial contacts with the office of the Minister of Fisheries about a particular case. It was the case of Mr. Wilfred White of Sandy Cove, Newfoundland, which is in my riding. He was one of many-and I have been told it is thousands-of fishermen across the country who through no fault of their own, but because of difficult circumstances and a
Fisheries Improvement Loans Act
desperate fishery for several years in a row, defaulted on their loans. This gentleman put all his personal moneys into the fishery and into making his loan payments. He sold off equipment and recreation vehicles to try to make his loan payments. He went down fighting, clinging by his fingernails to his boat and his gear. He tried to make a living and to make his payments. Nevertheless he went down. He had not borrowed the money for holidays, for personal aggrandizement or for luxuries. He borrowed the money for investment in the fishery. Having borrowed the money for that purpose, he said: "Thank God, at least the Government of Canada under the guaranteed fisheries improvement loan will see to the bad debt which now rests with the Bank of Nova Scotia".
What happened to Wilfred White, this man who clung on to the last instant, who invested every last dime to the last second trying to make a go of it in the fishery? What happened to his guaranteed federal government loan? He received a letter from the Bank of Nova Scotia which referred to his liaility under fisheries improvement loan No. 0669, granted on April 7, 1980, for $11,250. The bank confirmed that it forwarded its claim for loss to the Government of Canada and that its claim under period 6 was rejected. It went on to indicate that it had no other alternative but to look to Mr. White for liquidation of the debt.
I called the branch manager of the Bank of Nova Scotia on the northern peninsula of Newfoundland and asked: "What the hell is going on? Why are you threatening and sending in collection agencies to harass Wilfred White, an honest man, a decent man, and a good man"? The bank manager said: "I agree. He is an honest, decent and good man and I am embarrassed that I have to take this kind of action."
Oh, oh!
Members of the New Democratic Party may laugh and think it is funny that fishermen-
They lost the seat.

Yes, they lost the seat.-are trying to make a go of it in Newfoundland. They may laugh. They may think that the problems of the fishermen are no more than a matter to be chuckled at in this House. They may think that the representation I make on behalf of the fishermen of northern Newfoundland is inadequate and something to be laughed at. However, let me tell my colleague from the New Democratic Party that Wilfred White is only one of dozens in his community who has been-it is not too strong a word to say-shafted by this Government. Let us look at what the legislation we are extending today for six months says:
-to make any payment to any lender-
Lenders being banks:
-in respect of loss sustained by it as a result of a guaranteed loan made during the period-

December 15, 1986
Fisheries Improvement Loans Act
The wording of this legislation is misleading. It does not make any payment to any lender, the banks, with respect to any loss under guaranteed loans. The loans are not guaranteed. There is an escape clause. If you live in an area and deal with a bank where the economy is bad and where more than 10 per cent of the lenders have had to default at the 10 per cent level, the bank can stop receiving guarantees from the Government of Canada.
What if my colleague were a fisherman, received a loan and defaulted early, say the first time he got in trouble he gave up the ghost, went to the bank and said: "I default"? He gets his loan paid for by the Government of Canada because he is within the first 10 per cent of those to default. If my other colleague is a fighter, hangs on to the bitter end, struggles for a couple of years, not properly clothing, feeding or looking after his family in order to hang on, finally gives up, goes to the bank and says: "I have defaulted", they tell him that the first 10 per cent has been taken up and there is nothing they can do for him. What happens then?
Is it a question of having a bad credit rating? Is it a question of being embarrassed personally because you are in trouble with the bank? Fishermen are embarrassed. They have their pride.
Is that all it is? Is it a question of having great difficulty next time out getting a loan? Is that all it is? It is all of that, but much more, Mr. Chairman. It is a bank coming at you through a series of collection agencies out of St. John's, Halifax or Toronto, sending a notice to a fisherman in Sandy Cove, Newfoundland, a notice concerning his Government guaranteed loan, telling him that he better sell his truck, his house or whatever gear he has left with which to make a living for himself and his family and that he better scrape up $11,000 and repay the bank because the bank's books must be balanced. He must suffer the indignity of something less than a welfare regime because his so-called Government guaranteed loan is no guarantee at all.
That has been going on in record numbers, in particular in the last year, and I know the Minister is aware of it. It may have happened in previous years, but recently there has been a dramatic increase. The reason is that the Minister-it is not the Minister's fault-has inherited a fishery where in some parts of this country there have been four or five desperate years in a row. He has inherited fishermen who have been on their backs, trying to make a go of it for four or five years in a row, some of whom have finally buckled under the crushing burden of loan repayment. The Minister has been aware of this situation for a year.
I ask the Minister, as much as it is pleasant to see the basic concept of a fishermen's improvement loan extended for six more months because it would have run out otherwise, why it was not possible during the last year, when we Members of Parliament were aware of this problem, to have come forward with a new Bill today? Why have an extension to an existing problem that seeks to provide remedies to inherent injustice and unfairness?
I want an assurance from the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans that this Bill we pass today is not an exercise in fading out the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act over six months. I want a minimal assurance in expressing my disappointment that as we do not have a new Bill before us today that in six months he will come before us with a new Bill, one that will be relevant to existing circumstances evident in the fishery of eastern Canada and indeed in the fishery of the West Coast of Canada, in the Province of British Columbia.
I want the Minister to examine the plight of all of the Wilfred Whites of Canada, legitimate fishermen, honest people seeking to do an honest day's work and in the course of bringing in some new Bill to examine whether or not retroactively some kind of justice and sense of fairness can be introduced so that the unreasonable penalty that Wilfred White and many others have paid and are continuing to pay can somehow be rectified.
I, with my colleagues, support the notion that this Bill be extended for six months, but only because the concept of a fishermen's improvement loan is a good one and ought not to be lost. I cannot in good conscience-and I have written the Minister repeatedly on this issue-say that the Bill we are passing today is one that is worthy of the name Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, it is not. I beg the Minister of Fisheries of rectify this problem as quickly as possible.

Mr. Chairman, the Member has put a question and a proposal to me. I would like to respond to the suggestion that he has made. As the Minister responsible for all the fishermen of Canada, I certainly sympathize with the concerns of individual fishermen, such as Wilfred White and others whose particular adverse circumstances are brought to my attention from time to time.
I am somewhat disappointed that the Hon. Member was not able to be with us earlier when we commenced debate on Bill C-32. I understand that that was probably not possible. I did indicate that the six month period we are requesting, by way of an extension to the current loan period referred to as period nine, is not merely to find a way of amending the current Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, although that might be one consequence we will arrive at by the end of the next six months in 1987, but to look at other ways of consolidating and improving the provision of preferential financing for fishermen, whether it be through the Federal Business Development Bank, by consolidation with the Small Loans Act or perhaps even consolidation with the Farm Improvement Loans Act.
Those questions are currently being examined. I want to assure the Hon. Member, not in the context of the interpretation he places on the Nielsen task force recommendation, but with a view to improving the way in which we manage credit services for fishermen that the general thrust of this Government and this Minister is to improve the way in which we manage all the services of Government and the fishery.
I do not want to appear antagonistic in suggesting that the loan period, which is causing the difficulty for the Hon.
December 15, 1986

Member's fishermen in particular, was established by way of legislation adopted prior to July 1, 1977. Period six extended a certain ceiling on loans to be financed by the major chartered banks for the period July 1, 1977, to June 30, 1980. In that period an unprecedented number of loans were issued by the major banks, some $77 million worth. Then many of the fishermen who took out those loans for various kinds of vessel improvements, equipment, et cetera, discovered, in the early 1980s, that the crushing burden of high interest rates put them in a position where they could no longer meet their loan payments.
It was the double whammy of a high rate of lending by the banks, in period six in particular, and high interest rates. We found that portion of the loans guaranteed by the Government of Canada was less than all of the defaults over the last two years. I think all Hon. Members understand that. The reason for this is the formula contained in Section 6(2)(ii) of the Act. It requires that the Government guarantee will amount to only 90 per cent on the first $125,000, 50 per cent on the next $125,000 and 10 per cent on anything above that.
In effect, under the old legislation we are allowed to guarantee defaults to the extent of 10 per cent plus a 1 or 2 per cent correction out of a total portfolio of some $76 million. The number of individuals caught in this bind is not large, but I am looking for remedies for the cases we are dealing with. I must remind Hon. Members that we have to work co-operatively with provincial loan boards in this respect. That is one reason for the requested extension of period nine. We can in that time devise a better remedy for those extremely abnormal circumstances when interest rates take off as they did in the early 1980s.
I will conclude by urging the Hon. Member to support us in speedy passage of this Bill. Over the next six months we will attempt to make the necessary amendments, which must be done in consultation with fishermen, provincial loan boards and provincial Governments, and I undertake to do that. However, I must register the caveat that what comes out at the end of that process may not be just an improvement to this Act, it may be something else. I undertake to ensure that the something else is consistent with the need to continue to assist in the development of the fishery in an orderly and helpful way.

Mr. Chairman, I, too, support my colleagues in wanting to see this Bill passed quickly and I share in the comments just made by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe.
I want to use this opportunity, and I hope you will give me some latitude, to ask a question on an issue which is very important today to inshore fishermen in Newfoundland. I am glad to see the Minister of Employment and Immigration in the House. I hope he will listen to what I have to say because it applies particularly to him. I am sure the Minister of Fisheries
Fisheries Improvement Loans Act
and Oceans would be interested as well. If I could just get the attention of the Minister of Employment and Immigration?
It is a Liberal Member who is talking to him.

I want to tell the Minister about an existing situation and get his assurances on a certain matter. Because of a failure in the inshore fishery of Newfoundland, some $4 million was allocated to create work programs for those fishermen who did not qualify for unemployment insurance this winter as a result of the failure of the inshore fishery. That is much less than was allocated last year, which was $6 million. There have been radio reports in Newfoundland that only $1 million of that $4 million is to be taken up by fishermen because of the qualification restrictions put on it by the Department. If the radio reports are correct, and I hope they are not, then only a very small minority of the inshore fishermen who did not qualify through no fault of their own will qualify for unemployment insurance.
The Government of Canada has allocated some $800 million to farmers in western Canada and only $4 million for inshore fishermen in Newfoundland. I want an assurance from the Minister that all of that $4 million will be available and that those who do not qualify for unemployment insurance this year for those reasons will not be excluded from this program. Can the Minister give that assurance this afternoon?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I will allow the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans to answer that question but not the Minister of Employment and Immigration.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure the Hon. Member will understand it is probably more appropriate that I attempt to respond to his question. All I can say on behalf of my colleague and myself at this point is that we have had discussions since this problem developed with a view to using it, not exclusively but to a considerable measure, to assist those inshore fishermen. This will enable them to undertake projects which will be beneficial to themselves as fishermen and at the same time allow them to supplement their earnings in the way the Hon. Member has suggested. We will continue with those discussions. I can assure the Hon. Member that my colleague and I are both very sympathetic to the situation.
But what is the answer to the question?

Mr. Chairman, the Minister said that when he brings in legislation in six months it may be to this Act or it may be tied in with agricultural improvements or small business or some other package. Are the Minister and his Government committed to the idea that the fishing industry needs some kind of government guarantee loan program and that it should not simply be left to the mercy of market forces and the normal lending institutions, as the Nielsen task force suggests?

Mr. Chairman, we understand the special needs and circumstances of fishermen. Whether it be a federal

December 15, 1986
Fisheries Improvement Loans Act
Government guarantee program or some other form of special consideration, whatever evolves between now and the end of the six-month period will be of special benefit to ensure that fishermen can continue to finance their activities without being subject to the kind of perdition that he refers to. I am working closely with my colleagues to that end and we hope the program which evolves will be equally or more helpful and eliminate some of the problems we were debating earlier this afternoon.

Mr. Chairman, can the Minister indicate how he sees the future of this Act or its successor in relation to the Conservative Party's promise to bring in a SI00 million buyback program for the West Coast, which promise was made during the 1984 election campaign?

I am very pleased that the Hon. Member asked that question. He touches upon one of the strange paradoxes, of which there are many, in regard to the management of the fisheries. Over an extended period of time we have financed, on a preferential basis, the expansion of our fleet, in this case the West Coast salmon and herring fleet, largely through the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. Almost 50 per cent of the loans guaranteed under this program encouraged the expansion and modernization of that fleet. On the other hand, we have an acknowledged problem of excess capacity. This problem also exists in some areas of the Atlantic fisheries. It is alleged that this is one of the serious difficulties which we must confront in the southwest area of Nova Scotia in particular.
The new initiative, in whatever form it takes, must specifically recognize the fact that if the Government properly spends money to modernize the vessels and make them more efficient and safe, it should not be expected to buy them back when they become too efficient and there are too many of them. That is why, in these times of tight finances, I do not favour a direct government funded buy-back program, bearing in mind that the people of Canada have already contributed significantly through programs like FILA to the building of those vessels in the first place.
Just to be perfectly clear, is it correct that the 1984 election promise is, in the words of Richard Nixon, "inoperative"?

Mr. Chairman, if the Hon. Member examines what he considers to be a promise, I think he will find that the Progressive Conservative Party, running for election at that time, indicated that some fleet rationalization initiatives would have to be taken. From my perspective, there was never a promise that it would be funded by the general revenues of the people of Canada, although some initial funding would be required, as Dr. Peter Pearse recommended some time ago, to get such a program under way. My priority for the West Coast, as I have stated repeatedly, has been to produce more salmon rather than to buy out fishing boats and reduce the amount of employment available to fishermen. I believe we
should expand the resource upon which their livelihood is based.

Mr. Chairman, the Minister keeps referring to FILA and how great it is. I presume that is the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. Why would the Minister not amend the Bill presently before the House to change the 10 per cent to 15 per cent in order that the 1,000 fishing enterprises which were recently hit by the banks could have their loans guaranteed by the federal Government?
That is the problem with this Bill. There are fishermen in seven provinces who signed up under this Act for loans from banks. Lo and behold, when they could not pay their loans they sold the gear they had bought and the federal Government then refused to honour its guarantee to the banks. The Minister said that was because the banks had exceeded the 10 per cent specified in the Act.
This has never happened before in the history of the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, which dates back to the 1950s. It has never happened before that practically every bank and financial institution in Canada has been cut off from the federal guarantee. Practically every bank in the Minister's riding in British Columbia was notified by FILA that it had exceeded the 10 per cent. It makes no sense for the Minister to say that it was only the Bank of Montreal and the Bank of Commerce. It was also the Royal Bank and the Bank of Nova Scotia. The Royal Bank of Canada and the Bank of Nova Scotia should hang their heads in shame at the thought of the letters they sent out to hundreds of fishermen. One day those financial institutions will have to admit publicly what they did to fishing enterprises and families in British Columbia, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland, and on the north shore of Quebec.
My question to the Minister is very simple. The purpose of this Bill is to extend the period of time for six months. The last Bill which came before the House was for a one-year extension. All previous Bills were for three-year or five-year extensions. We are now going to extend it for six months, quite obviously to do away with it.
This has never happened before since the Act was adopted in the mid-1950s. Therefore why does the Minister not simply change the formula to get all the fishing enterprises off the hook with the banks? In other words, why does the Government of Canada not pay up the guarantees? The Government stood in the House the other day and claimed there was $1 billion for the farmers of Canada. Where is the paltry amount of money needed by the fishermen of Canada? They signed a piece of paper which said they were guaranteed by the federal Government. When they could not pay, they discovered that they were not guaranteed by the Government of Canada and had collection agencies, the courts and the banks down their necks.
I am told by FILA that there are 1,500 fishing enterprises in seven provinces involved in this. That is what they tell me but there are probably more than that. Take as an example a
December 15, 1986

fisherman who made $5,000 in 1986 and owes $30,000. He must put up all his property and remortgage his home. We have great pride in our banks, which have a great sense of community spirit and humanitarianism. The first thing they did was to send letters to all these people asking them to take out life insurance on their loans since the federal Government no longer guarantees them. Just imagine that, Mr. Chairman. That is the banks for you.
The Minister could get the banks off the hook. I do not like the letters which the banks sent out or the actions which they took. I received a dossier the other day from Nova Scotia containing some incredible letters. However, the banks are claiming ignorance of what was in the Act. They should have known what was in it. Why does the Minister not simply change the percentage in order that the federal Government can guarantee the loans which the fishermen thought were guaranteed by the Government when they signed at the bank? That is a pretty simple question. I do not know whether the Minister has Cabinet or Treasury Board authorization. However, would he entertain such an amendment to the Bill or support a special Cabinet order to pay those fishermen off since he is going to phase out the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act anyway?

Mr. Chairman, the Hon. Member knows that I do not have authorization to accept such an amendment and neither could I accept it. If the Member were in the banking business, whether in a private or public sector financial institution, he would never advocate that all loans in default be paid off by the proprietor. The reality is that in the 31 years since the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act was first adopted in 1955 until March 31 of this year, 18,000 loans were made. There have only been 611 claims paid to lenders for defaults at an average of $13,500.
The Hon. Member knows that when a fisherman undertakes an obligation to repay one of these loans, he will incur that obligation just as any other borrower, whether or not the bank received satisfaction under this Act. In other words, if the loan goes into default with the bank and the lender can claim against the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, the liability will remain in perpetuity with the fishermen because it remains a liability to the Crown. I do not believe the Hon. Member is advocating that in all cases fishermen merely have their defaults paid off by the Government of Canada. Why would we have a loan system in the first place which entails a certain obligation, indeed a written undertaking, to repay this amount?
I cannot accept the proposal. The Hon. Member has referred to some 1,500 fisheries enterprises, as he calls them, which are being impacted by this unfortunate development associated with loans entered into in the early part of the 1980s. However, he has never provided me with a list of such institutions, nor, I am told by my officials, is there a list that is anywhere near that magnitude of loans in default. I do not
Fisheries Improvement Loans Act
think it is appropriate for a Member to exaggerate and sow the seeds of antagonism toward the Government for a program that he adopted and approved as a member of the Government at that time. It is he and his colleagues opposite who set these limits and established the conditions under which these fishermen are now facing hardship.
In legitimate cases we will try, through adjustments to the form of assistance given to fishermen, to rectify these injustices. However, we cannot make the system wide open and promise to pay off all the loans of fishermen who have fallen into default. I hope the Hon. Member will appreciate that.

Mr. Chairman, I want to raise two matters. Those fishermen who had to put up their homes, their pick-up trucks and mortgage their lives because of this problem with the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act notified the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. In fact, I have countless numbers of letters which I can give the Minister. If he is saying that he would solve the problem if it existed, then let me tell him that there are seven in the community of Summerford in Notre Dame Bay, and there are 14 in Twillingate. The Minister should check the mail if he believes they do not exist. He should talk to the former Minister if he says that he has not received letters because that is where I obtained my letters. I have copies of each letter from the Minister.
The Minister asks why the Government of Canada should pay off the fisherman who has defaulted on his loan. What is the purpose of the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act if it is not to provide a guarantee to a fisherman who cannot pay off his loan? That is when the Act comes into force. The first thing a fisherman loses is the property he bought with the bank loan that was guaranteed by the federal Government. According to the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, for fishermen in the first 10 per cent, the difference between what the bank received on the sale of the property and what the fisherman received as a loan is paid by the federal Government. That is the purpose of the Act.
The Minister seems to be saying that regardless of whether the fisherman is in the first 10 per cent or the second 10 per cent, he should still owe the money to the federal Government. That may be legally correct, that there is no longer any debt because it is paid for by the federal Government. The Minister says that there are not 1,500 such cases in Canada and Hon. Members should not be allowed to state such figures. I suggest that the Minister should tell us exactly how many fishermen have been in this situation in the last two years. He cannot tell us that because he does not know. He does not know because he has no way of knowing. He simply notifies the banks that they have reached a limit and, for example, a letter to pay off Mr. Ron Jones in Summerford in Notre Dame Bay.
The Minister's Department sends a letter to the bank saying that the bank has reached the limit of its claims. The Minister has no way of knowing how many times the bank sends letters notifying the fishermen that they no longer honour their loans. The letters from the banks simply say that they have been

December 15, 1986
Fisheries Improvement Loans Act
informed by the federal Department of Fisheries and Oceans that those fishermen are no longer guaranteed under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act.
The House may recall that we presented the letters to the House over a year ago, showing exactly what was said. The Minister says that the numbers are wrong but he has no way of knowing the exact figure.
Do you know?

No, I do not know. However, estimates have been given to me and we have received complaints from seven provinces in Canada, including British Columbia. It is not only poor Newfoundland or the east coast of Newfoundland that are affected, but also British Columbia and other provinces.
The Government is ultimately the only body that can correct this situation unless the banks of Canada were to agree to forget about these defaulted payments. However, we know that when the banks deal with people like fishermen and farmers, they operate the same as collection agencies. In fact, I am surprised that banks across Canada have not opened collection agencies in their front offices to act on behalf of the Government of Canada and others.
There is a major flaw in the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. It only came to light in the past two years because the fishery was not as bad as it was in the mid and late 1970s. The Minister has made several speeches in this chamber in which he recognized that the fisheries were in difficulty and people could not pay their loans. We would certainly support the Minister if he were to assist the fishermen of Canada and introduce a change to guarantee all the loans.
The Minister is going to eliminate the provisions of this Act. As a final Christmas present to all those fishing enterprises that were notified by the banks, why not introduce a provision that will pay off their loans as well. That is the point I am attempting to make.

Mr. Chairman, I believe I detected a repetition of the previous question in the comments of the Hon. Member. I would like to respond to him as concisely as I can. The Hon. Member suggested that we somehow establish a loan program in which the people of Canada guarantee a certain portion of the liability and that it be a loan program not a grant program.
I remind Hon. Members that in the entire period of this program, since the first legislation was passed in 1955, the claims paid to the lending institutions have amounted to $13.5 million and the recovery of those claims has amounted to only $319,000. In other words, Mr. Chairman, the people of Canada have paid out $13.5 million against those claims in recognition of the liability of the Government of Canada. Those claims have been paid, but those fishermen who remain liable have only paid to the extent of $300,000. Therefore, we have virtually guaranteed at the point the bank pays off the loan that that is the last we will hear from the fishermen.
I do not believe the Hon. Member is suggesting we let everyone off scot-free. Why not call it a grant program, if that be the case? We believe that people who borrow money should accept some degree of responsibility for the repayment of the loan, as we do in the private banking industry. We accept that the Government should help out in a small way, as is done by the 1 per cent plus prime limit on the interest rate, but I do not think the Government can be expected to go a whole lot further in dealing with the small number of fishermen who, perhaps for reasons of misfortune, bad management or bad judgment, find themselves in a position of not being able to pay back.
When the Hon. Member throws numbers around such as "1,500 fishing enterprises", he is distorting and exaggerating to a serious degree. If the letters I have received are any measure of the number of cases where this is bringing hardship to fishermen, then those 20 or so letters I have received since I was appointed Minister would be a very small measure of the seriousness of this problem compared with the numbers the Hon. Member is throwing around.
I might also add that in the past two years we have seen a remarkable recovery in the fishing industry. Last year earnings were up 20 per cent over the previous year and landings were up 10 per cent. This year the performance will be just as remarkable. Foreign exchange earnings from the Atlantic fishery alone will exceed $2 billion this year. While it is true there will always be some unfortunate fishermen, particularly in the Hon. Member's province, about whom 1 am deeply concerned and will try to help in every way I can, there will nevertheless be cases which cannot be resolved merely by absolving the fishermen of their responsibility to pay back.
When the Hon. Member refers to the banking institutions, I share his concern, because we have found that some banks quickly exceeded their maximum liability and others did not. That suggests to me that perhaps some banks, or branches at least, have been more careless when a fisherman went into default in perhaps paying them off without a whole lot of hassle or a lot of attempt to collect. They consumed the maximum amount we could agree to under the formula which the Hon. Member's Government adopted and the fishermen have had to look somewhere else for assistance. Other banking institutions, and I will not name them, still have some of their access to guarantees unfulfilled. I will make a commitment to the Hon. Member that during the period of the next six months we will look at that situation. We will look at the extent to which some of the banks have not consumed all of their acccess to assistance under this program while others consumed their access very, very quickly.
I might add, Mr. Chairman, that in doing that we should not penalize those who have not consumed all of their access to guarantees under this program merely to advantage those banks which quickly came to the Government asking that a claim be made. Perhaps that focuses on one of the basic faults of the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, an Act, I repeat, that the Hon. Member stood in this House and approved. He
December 15, 1986

renewed those periods of loan guarantees probably two or three times in his time in the House as a member of the Government. Now we have this problem today which suggests there is a basic flaw in the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. We are not asking for a two-year extension, only six months, because we intend to correct that situation.

Mr. Chairman, the problem with foreclosures in the 1,500 cases which I said were in existence in seven provinces came up only in the past couple of years because the banks were notified by the Government of Canada that loans which were taken out in the 1970s and early 1980s had gone over their limit. A fisherman owning a boat is called an "enterprise", for the Minister's benefit, which is the terminology used by the banks. The fisherman stopped making payments on his loans and, of course, his property was taken and sold, which is the normal procedure. Then a claim was made by the bank to the federal Government, which is also the normal procedure under this guarantee. Therefore, it took that period of time.
The Minister says I am exaggerating and distorting the numbers. How does he know I am exaggerating and distorting the numbers when he does not know the numbers? Neither does his adviser, the expert sitting in front of him. No one knows what the numbers are.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I would hope that the Hon. Member's statement would be directed just to the Minister.

Mr. Chairman, I thought the Minister would want to check it out with someone. The fact is that the banks are notified in a letter from the Department of Fisheries that they have exceeded their guarantee limit with the federal Government. The banks then take over and notify the fishermen. It has nothing to do with the Minister of Fisheries nor the Department of Fisheries. I predict the Minister will rise in a moment and say: "We have asked the financial institutions from time to time about the numbers of loans we cannot collect", but he cannot be accurate on the numbers.
A year ago I took the number of representations we had and contacted the banks concerned. We came up with a general figure. That figure we came up with a year ago has now, I am sure, been exceeded because I am positive that even more people have started to default. Therefore, the numbers keep growing. The Minister can verify this, but I believe it takes some 15 years before we know just how balanced the books are with respect to the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act.
Therefore, I go back to the original question. The Minister says earnings are up 20 per cent and landings are up 10 per cent. Yes, Mr. Chairman, the landings were up on those big offshore boats, the landings on codfish on the East Coast and everywhere else was up. National Sea Products went up on the stock market. If one wants to make money these days, one would go with National Sea Products because it was given the factory freezer trawler licences by the federal Government.
Fisheries Improvement Loans Act
Yes, the landings went up and will keep going up for National Sea Products and the other companies. However, landings are down for the inshore fishermen. The Minister of Fisheries has not been around long enough to know what we call an inshore fishery. Although the Department of Fisheries says so, an inshore fisherman is not a fellow with a herring or cabling licence who has a 50-foot boat. In our books, he is not an inshore fisherman because he was able to sell to the fish plants this summer.
The inshore fishermen, the fellows with 18, 20, 25 and 30-foot boats could not sell to the fish plants. There was no big amount of money coming to them. The fishing industry's council or whatever it is, the Economic Council of Canada, the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council, the Newfoundland Minister of Fisheries and the federal Minister of Fisheries are all saying what a marvellous year 1986 was since landings were up. The poor fishermen all along the coast of Newfoundland are saying: "Are these fellows in Mexico? Are they from another world? From where are they operating? They must have their heads in the sand". Of course, on the books landings were up but they were not up for the inshore fishermen, the ones who take advantage of these fisheries improvement loans. Many of them got stuck because the federal Government's guarantee was not enough.
Granted, this measure was brought in when the Liberals were in power. It was brought in in the 1950s. It was redone in the 1960s and the 1970s. The last time it was redone was a year ago when this Government was in power. The formula was brought in by the Liberals, true, but the Bill before the House changes the Act. All I am asking is while the Minister is doing that, why does he not change the formula and backdate it to take care of those fishermen? The Minister says that there are not 1,500 of those fishermen. If the number is so small, why not amend the Bill and take care of those few fishermen. Maybe then I will let the Bill go through.

Mr. Chairman, I am interested in this legislation, particularly as it applies to the fishing industry in the Great Lakes. Not only are fishermen there having difficulties, but they are also having trouble maintaining wharfs and facilities because of the extremely high water level from which the Great Lakes are suffering. For instance, I am told that in the Lake Huron, Lake Erie and Lake St. Clair area, 55 of the 88 wharfs in small craft harbours are in serious disrepair due to the high water. Still the Department maintains an incredibly low amount of support, some $2.5 million, toward maintaining those wharfs not only in Ontario but in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and the Northwest Territories. Those provinces have all been gathered under the umbrella of small craft harbours which works out of Burlington.
If fishermen will not have to spend all their fisheries improvement loans on fixing government wharfs, it is essential that the Department provide additional funding. I know the Minister has been concerned about this issue. He has received

December 15, 1986
Adjournment Motion
many representations from our side of the House, from his own side of the House and from members of the NDP.
I hope the Minister might be able to give us an indication of just what is the situation with regard to small craft harbours. Besides renewing this legislation which is essential, will the Minister be able to improve the wharfs at places like South Baymouth, Meldrum Bay, Spanish, Hilton Beach, Richard's Landing, Little Current, Desbarats and Blind River, all of which support fishing and small craft activity?
I would like to know if the Minister will be able to provide a program of recovery and rehabilitation for those 55 wharfs in small craft harbours which have been damaged by the high water this past year or two. I wonder if he will be able to get the additional support and assistance required to carry out those improvements. I am told that it would require several million dollars over and above the regular maintenance budget so I hope the Minister will be given the latitutde to indicate to the millions of people who live in that area of Ontario and the West, people who depend on small craft harbour grants from the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, that they will receive moneys for the improvements which are so desperately needed.
We note from a recent report from Michigan that President Reagan has declared some 22 counties in the State of Michigan as disaster areas. The three levels of Government in the U.S. have committed some $10 million for flood improvement to small craft harbours and coastal areas. I hope that we might be able to receive the same kind of assistance in the Ontario region from the small craft harbours department which, of course, is a vital part of the Minister's Department of Fisheries and Oceans.

Mr. Chairman, I have a brief reaction to that. I think all Hon. Members would like to see the legislation before us wound up quickly. I gather there are other important items that we might debate this afternoon as well.
The Hon. Member is concerned about the high water levels in the Great Lakes. I certainly must consider seriously the damage that has been caused and it appears that in the foreseeable future, there will be no immediate turnaround. We cannot expect the water level to drop by three feet in the next 12 months. I am looking very seriously at special means of dealing with the situation. I hope early in the new year to bring in a report on it.

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans) moved
speechtext: that Bill C-32, an Act to amend the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, be read the third time and passed.

Mr. Speaker, as was explained during committee stage of this Bill, I and other Hon. Members have serious reservations about what is happening in the fishing community as it relates to moneys that were supposedly guaranteed by the federal Government and were then not paid because of a formula that triggered in when times were bad.
I suppose holding up this piece of legislation would not do any good, although I can tell you that I have a good mind to do that. As you know, on third reading there is unlimited time to speak on a Bill. I was thinking of it a moment ago as it relates to fishermen, and in the few remarks that I will make, I wish to explain why.
Many Members of this House represent the personal problems of fishermen. A great many Members in this Chamber have represented fishermen over the past two years in trying to deal with this problem of the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, and the notification from the banks that loans were no longer guaranteed under the Act. A typical case is a call from a fisherman who would state: "I have just received a letter from the bank saying I owe them $20,000, and I have $2 in my bank account. What am I going to do?" A letter would be received that stated: "The bank notifies me
December 15, 1986

they want full payment of $20,000 because that is the difference between what my gear has sold for and what I totally owe that bank, although, when I went into the bank, there was a sign that said 'Get a fisheries improvement loan guaranteed by the federal Government'".
The Minister has said that there are only a few of those fishermen. Nothing that we say to the Minister will make him change his mind and modify this Bill to take care of those few fishermen who were dealt such a back-handed slap by the Government and the financial institutions.
It is all too common now to see cases where fishermen have had to pay money back to the Government, to the banks under fisheries improvement loans, and who are stuck in a very bad financial situation. I had a few cases the other day that were rather shocking. For example, I had cases of 34 fishermen referred to me. They had won their cases three weeks ago before the Federal Court in Ottawa against the Unemployment Insurance Commission. They had been fighting for about six or seven years and had finally won their cases against the federal Government. The judge ruled that the fishermen won their cases. The Unemployment Insurance Commission took the decisions from all of these court cases three weeks ago, and decided that the fishermen did not win their cases. It is not going to pay up what the fishermen had already paid in.
As an example, Mr. Speaker, I will read from the case of Eric Keats, appellant, and the Minister of National Revenue, respondent; and the case of Anthony Burke, appellant, and the Minister of National Revenue, respondent. This was a judgment handed down by Mr. Justice Trahan three weeks ago in which the judge states that he has no alternative but to grant the appeals. Justice Trahan states: "It is ordered and adjudged that the determination by the Minister-be reversed". This is on the Unemployment Insurance Act. The judge further states;
I have nothing but admiration for Mr. Eric Atkinson, solicitor for the respondent, for the way in which he took the decision, with the authorization of the Minister of National Revenue, to ask the court to grant the Appeals-
After reading that, Mr. Speaker, one would have to say, "My goodness, the appellant won the case". But, oh, no, not with this Government. Not with the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, the Unemployment Insurance Commission, and the Department of National Revenue. No. Now they are saying the fishermen did not win their cases.
In looking at the cases that go to the courts regarding the fisheries improvement loans, that judgment is not being considered in favour of the fishermen at all. You find that some of the same people who were granted appeals under the Unemployment Insurance Act were nailed with loans that they had taken out under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act.
I have 34 cases here from three weeks ago. On each one I phoned the Unemployment Insurance Commission and was told that the Unemployment Insurance Commission was not going to pay because it felt it had won. It feels that its lawyers in the Unemployment Insurance Commission are the foremost authority. They know what they are doing. The lawyers in the
Fisheries Improvement Loans Act
Unemployment Insurance Commission know what they are doing. "We will not pay back these poor fishermen the money that they paid and the fines they paid because we believe that the judge meant to rule in favour of the Government of Canada here in the Federal Court three weeks ago."
I went over each of the 34 cases. Apparently, there are 121. But I went over the 34 cases, and I found out what the Government was claiming as the phrase that made it decide it won. The judge states:
I have no alternative but to grant the Appeals 83-560 (UI) and 83-508 (UI) according to the submission brought forth by the Respondent's Solicitor.
According to the judge, the respondent's solicitor had asked the court to grant the appeals. The judge then turned around and sent to every single one of these fishermen a judgment that stated: "It is ordered and adjudged that the determination by the Minister-be reversed-"
The point is that the Government is seen to be an awfully cold body of people as it relates to the fishermen of eastern Canada. It appears that the Government has said to the Departments, "Look, let's find every way possible to save money". When the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act comes up it states, "Let's get rid of it". It says that because it feels the same thing could be done under the Small Businesses Loans Act as is done under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. It even says that the same can be done by the Federal Business Development Bank as is done under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. Nothing could be further from the truth. It cannot be done. If you read this Act, you see that it is directed toward fishermen. The Small Businesses Loans Act is not directed toward fishermen at all, and neither is FBDB. Looking at the reference to FBDB, now there is something. Fishermen applying under FBDB to buy a new engine? Sure. They could apply this year and it would probably be dealt with in 1990.
The Government is searching for ways to save money. There were three people who worked in the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act administration, and now there is one. That is all. Of course, when this Act is done away with in six months time, they may still have somebody there because some of these loans will be in effect for at least 15 years.
To leave these fishermen high and dry and to say in the case of people who had received loans that some of them are covered by federal Government guarantee and others are not covered by a federal loan guarantee is not good enough.
It depended upon the point in time a fishermen came into the bank and said that he could not make any more payments. However, the fellow who tossed it up in the air and said that he would quit the fishery benefited. Rather than work like a slave looking for fish, he walked into the bank with his fisheries improvement loan, guaranteed by the federal Government, and said that he would not try for another year. He was paid. It was the fellow who struggled to make his payments and just barely made it who found himself high and dry, with collection

December 15, 1986
Coastal Fisheries Protection Act
agencies down his neck day and night. He was the fellow who was brought to court and had his property seized.
There is no way the Minister can know the number of fishermen who were so affected by the fault in the Act. It only happened since the Government came into office two years ago. The Minister notified the banks about the cut off of the loans, affecting every fisherman who claimed thereafter. The Government of Canada notified only the banks.
A little over a year ago we calculated the figures given to us by the banks and found that it involved 1,500 fishing enterprises in seven Canadian provinces. I dare say that that number has risen by the hundreds. After notification by the Government the banks notified fishermen that they must obtain life insurance on their loans. They did not need it before because the loans were guaranteed by the federal Government. They called them all in, even the ones who were honouring their loans. They were called in or received letters indicating that they needed insurance on their loans. The banks simply said that the federal Department of Fisheries would no longer honour the loans. On top of that there was the climate in the fishing community, with a report coming in saying that their loans under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act would now be taken away, terminated, and folded into the FBDB or the Small Businesses Loans Act. There is now talk that their unemployment insurance will be affected as well. Actions such as this are happening now.
As I mentioned earlier a group of fishermen, over 100 of them, have fought for seven years before appeal boards and before the courts. Finally 34 of them won their cases in black and white from a justice of the Federal Court, and the Unemployment Insurance Commission turned around and said: "No, we do not think you won". It was in black and white that they won, but they were required to appeal. They did not have any money to hire lawyers. These fishermen were represented by Members of Parliament who were doing it free because they were representing their constituents.
The general attitude of the Government of Canada toward fishermen leaves a lot to be desired. This is why I said to the Hon. Member for Egmont (Mr. Henderson), the official fisheries critic, that I had in mind to rise at third reading and not sit down. I had in mind to hold up the Bill all night, tomorrow, and the next day until Christmas, and then it would be too late. I know of cases similar to the fisheries improvement cases in which the federal Government said that they had not won their cases before the Federal Court although it was in black and white that they did. Again it was the heavy hand of the federal Government. As the Hon. Member for Egmont said, at least this is an extension of the fisheries improvement loans for six months. He indicated that I would not make it any better or worse by talking all night, all day tomorrow, and all day the next day.
They will ram it through anyway.

Yes, they will ram it through. However, it is enough to make one mad. These cases involve some of my
constituents and of course constituents from other parts of Canada. The heavy hand of the Unemployment Insurance Commission and the heavy hand of the federal Government came down on these poor, unfortunate fishermen with whom the judge agreed in their cases before the Federal Court after seven years of fighting.
We must find some way to right this wrong. I do not know how, unless we ask the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) who acted on behalf of the federal Government to rise in the House and explain. Did he lose these cases? That is what the judge said. If he says he lost them, then he will have to pay all fishermen in eastern Canada. The Minister of National Revenue is a good lawyer. He knows how to read a judge's decision. Perhaps I will ask him that question tomorrow or the next day to see what he says and to see whether he is on the side of fishermen and on the side of justice in society.
Again I ask the Minister of Fisheries, in re-examining the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, to look at those poor, unfortunate people who have had their property and everything else seized by the banks, all because they did not come in yesterday-they came in today-to get their loans guaranteed. They thought they had a guarantee from the Government.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the third time and passed.
