Mr. Chairman, I have no intention of opposing the legislation before us or of holding it up, for that
December 15, 1986

matter. However, I have some very serious questions for the Minister. As a matter of fact, I think we should congratulate him for the initiative which he is showing in this regard. I think it is a good move that penalties in the offshore are being increased. It is a measure which I applaud. We required that enforcement in that foreign fishermen or foreign ships cannot feel that they can come into Canadian waters with impunity. I fully support the actions of the Minister in this regard.
The Minister is doing something right, but everything he has done has not been right. I should like to ask him some questions about some of those other areas while we are on the topic because they are of great concern to fishermen in my riding. When we were dealing with the last Bill, the Hon. Member for Egmont mentioned the question of small craft harbours and the serious deterioration of many wharfs and breakwaters in fishing communities. I want to raise with the Minister the particular case of Lance au Loup in my riding in southern Labrador where $1 million was allocated for the improvement of a regional wharf for long liners in the straits area.
The wharf is half done. We have 12 or 15 long liners and 12 or 15 small fishing boats depending on that marine facility. It is incomplete and it is indicative of what has been happening. Attention has to be paid to our small craft harbours. We must have adequate funds. I remember very clearly one of the things our Party did when in government was to put adequate funds into small craft harbours. I remember one year in which $60 million-probably in the middle 1970s-was allocated to small craft harbours. We had a minimum of $30 million a year. That was before inflation overtook the present budget. The Minister has to address the issue that you cannot carry on a fishing industry if you do not have the proper wherewithal. It is like trying to sell automobiles without a garage. It cannot be done and the Minister has to pay attention, particularly to Lance au Loup.
There are two other issues I want to raise with the Minister, both of which he will know about, and I hope he will respond to them. The first is the situation at La Scie. La Scie is in a Catch-22 situation. The Minister, following along with the policy of our Party when we were the Government, brought in, according to the Kirby recommendations, what is known as the resource short plant program. That program is to assist those small communities and fish plants on the northeast coast of Newfoundland and elsewhere that do not get an adequate supply of fish from the inshore fishery. It is to have a supply of offshore fish landed at the small inshore plants, making them viable and keeping them going for a longer period of the year. Also, if a plant belongs to a company which has an offshore fleet, it cannot qualify for the resource short plant program. That is the situation in which La Scie finds itself.
It is interesting to know that La Scie was built, I believe, by the Government of Canada, many years ago. It is a community of about 3,000 people and serves a whole peninsula. The
Coastal Fisheries Protection Act
economy of the whole of the Baie Verte peninsula depends on that regional plant. I draw that to the Minister's attention because there is no way the community of La Scie can survive on inshore fish alone. La Scie has to have an allocation of offshore fish. I would ask the Minister to either amend the resource short plant program guidelines so that La Scie can be accommodated or allocate a supply of fish from elsewhere.
There was a proposal, for example, to allocate fish from a new facility that was built on the Labrador coast called Punchbowl, but nothing happened. That community and indeed the whole peninsula, which happens to be not only in my riding but in the riding of the provincial Minister of Fisheries, is in jeopardy because it does not have an adequate supply of fish. I hope the Minister will give us an answer of substance as to what he intends to do about this problem.
Third is an issue which we have raised with him and with his predecessor before. It also flows out of the Kirby task force report, namely, the concept of a northern fisheries development corporation. The Minister will know that in certain areas of the northern peninsula of Newfoundland and along the coast of Labrador we have marginal plants. These plants in small communities cannot survive because they are not part of a multinational organization but are simply small community plants.
Kirby's idea was to put those marginal plants together in what he described as a northern fisheries development corporation and to allocate federal funds, management and marketing expertise. If that were done in a collective way, the aggregate would be stronger than the parts that make it up. Each of those plants would benefit by being part of a larger cooperative effort, but that did not happen. When in Government our Party set aside $15 million to improve some of those plants and to set up that over all northern fisheries development corporation. Nothing has happened. The money has gone elsewhere. In the meantime, small plants are still struggling. I have not seen any better answer come along, neither have I seen any alternative action taken. I say to the Minister one of two things: either come up with a better idea and put it into effect or put in place the northern fisheries development corporation. The situation will not get better, it will only get worse.
The Minister will know that evidently the stocks we thought were off the shores of Newfoundland and Labrador in 2J and 3KL are not as strong as everybody thought them to be. The resource is not there that we thought was there. Everyone will have to tighten his belt a little. That means even more belt tightening for people who are in the position that I have described. Small marginal plants are at an even greater disadvantage because of weakness in the stocks.
Will the Minister follow through now by setting up the northern fisheries development corporation for the northern peninsula and for the coast of Labrador or will he come up with some alternative suggestion about how those particular plants are supposed to operate and maintain viability in the face of the factors I have just described?

Mr. Chairman, I believe that all Hon. Members would like to see these amendments to the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act adopted today as January 1 will represent the tenth anniversary of the extension by Canada of our offshore fisheries boundary to 200 miles. I think it is particularly timely and important that we recognize the prevalence of overfishing in the area at the limit of the 200 mile boundary and beyond. Through the introduction of improved surveillance methods, improved means of enforcement, higher fines and penalties, we hope to take greater control of those precious groundfish stocks, especially as they pertain to the Province of Newfoundland, in the area known as the nose and tail of the Grand Banks. I am urging and asking all Members to be as co-operative as they can.
At this point I want to compliment my colleague, the Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs who is in the House today. Without his leadership and co-operation we would not have been able to make significant announcements in the month of June which encompassed the measures before the House today, which were among a number of important new initiatives to toughen up and improve enforcement of those stocks for the benefit of Atlantic Canadian fishermen. I will make further comment at third reading stage, assuming we have time at the end.
I will concisely respond to the questions asked by my colleague. He asked me to give some indication of the future of the small craft harbours program, and how we intend to handle the situation of La Scie in his riding. He asked also about the status of the northern fisheries development corporation, which was an outgrowth of the Kirby task force review and is a commitment which this Government made some time ago and which we have not yet fulfilled.
The Member is correct when he indicates that the Government of which he was a part increased significantly the funding for small craft harbours. That took place in particular in the years 1983 and 1984.1 do not want to criticize the Hon. Member or his Government for raising the budget for small craft harbours from about $42 to $44 million to $60 million during those two years, but I think it is reflective of what has been wrong in the management of our small craft harbour program.
If you go back over the history of that program since the responsibility to maintain those wharfs and harbours was changed from the Department of Public Works to the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, you will see that before every election a big shot of funding was made and brand new facilities were built. The problem is that over the past 30 years from the post-war period, there has been no ongoing budget to manage, maintain and dredge all of the 2,200 harbours across Canada for which I am responsible.
The Hon. Member knows there were certain references in the Throne Speech. We have been promising for some months a new policy approach to management of those harbours so as
to involve the fishermen more directly in the decisions on priorities and equipment purchase as well as the provision of services. We want to use available labour closer to home and at the same time overcome a number of deficiencies resulting from deterioration of those harbours. What I undertake to the Hon. Member is that we will put in place a new management regime which will not only deal with the necessary expansion and improvement to breakwaters and wharfs, but over the long term will allow us to improve general maintenance and eliminate safety-related deficiencies. I must tell him that we cannot do that at the present level of funding, but I am working toward major improvements in that area.
With respect to the La Scie situation, the Hon. Member knows that last year a competition was held to determine who would operate the new fish buying and servicing centre known as Punchbowl on the Labrador coast. One of the bidders was National Sea Products on behalf of the plant at La Scie. For reasons relating to the nature of their bid in relation to that of the Saltfish Corporation and one other bidder, they did not succeed in gaining the right to buy fish at Punchbowl and deliver it to La Scie as they intended. I undertake to the Hon. Member to reconsider the eligiblity of the plant at La Scie in the coming year because the program will be up for grabs again in 1987.
Finally, on the question of the northern fisheries development corporation, I am very conscious of the necessity for finding improved ways to expand the economy of Labrador and northern Newfoundland in order to help many of those marginal communities whose existence is dependent on the seasonal fishery, the inshore fishery in particular, and for whom the greater part of the year offers little opportunity and little hope. I am giving very careful attention to ways to embody the northern fisheries development corporation concept in a new initiative but not necessarily by creating yet another Crown corporation.
I do not believe the solution to problems is necessarily to be found in creating new institutions. We have to define our goals and objectives and then develop a plan to achieve them. I am giving serious thought to this and working co-operatively with the Newfoundland Minister of Fisheries. I hope to have something soon which the Hon. Member will see as a satisfying response to the undertaking made and a way of offering hope and increased economic opportunity to the people in his riding.

Mr. Chairman, I am glad to make a few comments on Bill C-26, an Act to amend the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act, and raise a few questions with him about it. The Act increases the fines payable by foreign vessels who transgress Canadian fishing regulations. That is something all Members of this House support. Unfortunately, it has become a necessity in the last few years.
The American poet, Charles Olson, in his Maximus poems, said that fishing was our first wild west. That was certainly true in the early years when Basque and Bretton fishermen
December 15, 1986

were coming over to the Grand Banks. There were occasional disputes and sometimes violence. Over a period of time there was, however, a sense that there was enough for everyone and a reasonable regime developed so that fishing disputes were settled without violence. Unfortunately, that seems to have broken down in the last few years because of increased pressure upon the resource by other countries as well as the increased needs of Canadian fishermen.
As the Minister pointed out, 10 years ago we unilaterally extended our economic zone to 200 miles. However, some areas of the Grand Banks, the nose and tail, are still outside of that zone. They are lucrative areas for other countries to fish. They also provide some temptation for foreign fishermen to sneak into the 200-mile economic zone of Canada in a form of piracy and literally rob us of our fish. Last spring we had the rather exciting spectacle of Canadian fisheries officers being kidnapped by Spanish fishing vessels and that resulted in an exciting sea chase and so on. That sort of thing should not happen and the legislation we have before us today is intended to prevent it from happening again.
There are two needs to be dealt with in this situation. First there is the short-term need for some tough measures, such as those announced by the Minister last June. These increased fines are a part of those measures. We need to be tough in enforcing the fisheries regulations for foreign vessels. On that basis we are fully prepared to support the increase in fines. Of the other measures announced by the Minister, some of them are regrettable but obviously necessary.
Second, we have the need to return to the rule of law and reason. We can all agree that the best kind of police force is that which never needs to use weapons and force. In fact, the best kind of police force is one that does not even need to be seen, but where people know the rule of law exists and will be enforced. I hope the Minister and other members of the Government are able to work toward an international civilized approach to our fish stocks so that we can eliminate the present situation where we have to play cops and robbers and act like a beleaguered corner store operator worried about a hold-up. That kind of thing is no more healthier on the international scene than it is in the corner store. Canada has developed some reasonable regulations and we would like to see them used on an international basis.
The Leader of the Newfoundland NDP suggested that the 200-mile zone should be extended unilaterally to take in the nose and tail of the Grand Banks. That suggestion was picked up by the Premier of Newfoundland and brought to the First Ministers' Conference. I understand a committee was established to look into that. I would be interested in knowing the status of that committee. Has it been set up? Who is on it? What are its terms of reference? When can we expect some answers from it?
Second, it is not enough for us to just raise the maximum fine. There has to be some way of getting the message through to the courts that they have to raise the level of fines they are imposing because in some parts of eastern Canada the courts
Coastal Fisheries Protection Act
are imposing very low fines when compared to the current maximum. If we are going to raise the maximum, we must send a message to our courts that international fisheries violations are serious enough that they should be considering imposing the maximum fines in a number of those cases.
Third, I would appreciate it if the Minister could bring us up to date on some of the measures he announced last June 13. In particular, he said that the Government would be arming DFO Atlantic offshore patrol vessels and boarding parties. I would like to know what is happening with that. He said the Government would be exloring with DND and MOT means of increasing dedicated air and sea surveillance, acquiring one dual engine helicopter for sea patrols, and developing an electronic fishing licence which will facilitate identification of licensed vessels. I would appreciate some update as to what is happening in those areas. Again, I want to indicate our general support for this measure.

Mr. Chairman, as I indicated earlier, at the end of third reading debate I will give an overview of why the Government is proceeding in this fashion. However, I will now deal with the Member's specific questions. First, he asks about the discussions which arose from the First Ministers' Conference held in Halifax in November, 1985. At that time, driven largely by the strongly held views of the Province of Newfoundland that we should do more to show our commitment to manage and maintain the stocks on the Grand Banks for the benefit of Atlantic Canadian fishermen, it was decided that federal and provincial Ministers responsible for fisheries would meet and develop a strategy for dealing with this general problem of foreign-overfishing, both within and beyond the present 200-mile fishing zone.
As a result of that, I met with provincial Ministers first in St. John's in January, 1986, and subsequently on more than a half dozen occasions. This led to a proposed course of action on the management and enforcement of regulations for the offshore fisheries. As well, we reached a very high degree of understanding and agreement on issues as diverse as aquaculture, the quality of our fish products and marketing initiatives, and international trade.
When we presented our report at the First Ministers' Conference in November of this year in Vancouver, it represented a unanimous series of recommendations to our respective governments on ways to enhance the economic benefit and employment created by our fisheries in all parts of Canada. This referred to the recreational fishery as well as the commercial. It gave attention to the potential for the shore-based processing industry to grow and to improve the quality of our products.
There was one question left unresolved at the meeting in Vancouver. That was the dilemma of how to gain increased control over the groundfish stock, particularly the precious northern cod stock which swims back and forth within and beyond the 200-mile fishing limit at the extremities of the

December 15, 1986
Coastal Fisheries Protection Act
Grand Banks known as the nose and the tail of the Grand Banks. We believe and have argued at the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries Association that those resources are really a part of Canadian stocks which live a significant part of their lives within the Canadian 200-mile economic limit and that they, therefore, should be managed from the perspective of conserving and enhancing them for the benefit of Canadian fishermen by Canada.
For that reason, the Government of Newfoundland has advocated that the boundary be extended to encompass the nose and tail of the Grand Banks. For reasons of complexity of law and international diplomacy, it is not feasible now or in the foreseeable future, from the standpoint of precedents in law, for Canada to extend that boundary. However, the Premier of Newfoundland proposed to the Prime Minister and other Premiers in Vancouver that we establish a special working group to study ways and means to give effect to that which we desire, that is, to enhance our ability to manage those resources, which we believe to be Canadian resources, for the benefit of Canadian fishermen. The proposal was that only when they are surplus to our own requirments would they be shared with foreign nations and that we should find ways to improve the effectiveness with which we manage those resources whether or not it is possible to extend the boundary which, at the present time, does not seem possible.
The Hon. Member also asked for specifics about other aspects of the announcements I made in St. John's, Newfoundland, on June 13. We are dealing today with the issue of significantly increasing the fines for violations of the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act by both foreign and Canadian vessels. Canadian vessels are singled out in the Act with regard to the practice of buying Fish from a foreign vessel and transporting it into Canadian waters, that being clearly illegal under the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act. Today we are dealing with significant increases in the penalties for such offences as well as for foreign vessels which illegally enter the Canadian zone.
We are in the process of selecting a twin-engine helicopter which will operate from the pads on our two major offshore coastal patrol vessels on the Grand Banks, those being the Leonard J. Cowley and the Cape Roger. We are well advanced in the preparation of a Treasury Board submission for the purpose of acquiring that helicopter which will effectively extend the range and the ability to give early warning to fishing vessels which are violating our fishing boundaries. The area which those very costly patrol vessels can surveil will be extended by a factor of three or four.
We will also be committing funding to obtain fixed-wing high-altitude surveillance support from a private operator with a specially instrumented aircraft for monitoring offences of our coastal fishing zone. We will continue to enjoy the support of the Department of National Defence which has made available significant hours of surveillance using the tracker aircraft, the Aurora aircraft based in Greenwood, Nova Scotia, and destroyers. In each case a certain number of
hours are made available to the Department of Fisheries and Oceans for such surveillance.
With regard to the arming of patrol vessels, the armaments have been purchased. The training is in process and very comprehensive and carefully considered rules of engagement are being established to ensure that these armaments are used to show that we intend to uphold the provisions of the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act, but in the most responsible way as all Canadians would expect such armaments to be used in the defence of our fishing zone.
The final aspect of the announcements dealt with the development of an electronic fishing licence. This would be somewhat like an emergency location transmitter on an aircraft. However, rather than sending out only a single tone, it would send out a code which would convey the number of the fishing licence carried by that vessel. Any foreign vessel found fishing in Canadian waters which was not emitting this electonic signal would be in clear violation and would be pursued and, hopefully, apprehended for illegal fishing. We are requesting proposals from the private sector for the development of such an electronic fishing licence. The technology is not complicated. It is an adaptation of an existing technology. We are encouraging the submission of proposals for the development of such a system.
I have probably elaborated at greater length than the Hon. Member expected, but I hope my comments have been helpful.

Mr. Chairman, I listened to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans with great interest. I do not know whether to agree with the intent of the Bill. Some may say that one would have to agree with increasing the fines for those people who violate our fishing laws, but it is morally wrong for the Government to watch as the French fleet, in the vast area south of Newfoundland and east of Nova Scotia, take four times their allocation this year. They were allocated 7,600 tonnes of fish and the metropolitan fleet from France took 26,000 tonnes in the area that goes over 200 miles down from Newfoundland to the mid-Atlantic. There was not one observer aboard those boats. However, if a Canadian overfishes his quota, the boat is hauled in and he is arrested.
The Minister can say that there is a legal dispute with the Government of France, but that does nothing about the fact that the total allowable catch on the south coast of Newfoundland and eastern Nova Scotia was surpassed this year. What did the Minister do about this? He cut back on the Canadian quota so that Canadian fishermen have a quota on the East Coast that is less than last year's quota. Meanwhile, the French continue to overfish to the point they are four times their quota for the East Coast of Canada.
Let us consider another flaw in the Bill. The Minister talks about preserving the stocks on the nose and the tail of the banks. I will give him some credit for the fact that he got an agreement from NAFO that no one would fish in some of
December 15, 1986

those areas. This means that a Canadian fisherman fishing in those areas would be charged. However, if a Spanish or Portuguese boat fished these areas, there would be a diplomatic note from NAFO to that country, alerting it to the fact that it is not allowed to fish in this area. Furthermore, the United States does not come under NAFO and therefore can put its entire fleet in that area. Canadians will be fined for fishing in that area. The Americans, who are not part of NAFO, are there now, as well as the Koreans. The Spanish fished in this area three weeks ago and were sent a diplomatic note.
The fact that the Minister cannot arrest American fishermen who go to this area angers many boat owners on the East Coast of Canada. Yet, the Government brings in a Bill that increases the fine for Newfoundlanders. The other day, a fisherman was arrested because his boat was 49 feet 11.5 inches long. If his boat was 50 feet long he could have received a quota. The skipper of the boat was from Newfoundland and the boat came from Conception Bay. The skipper is known as Blackie and people from Nova Scotia will know about whom I am talking. He was 202 miles off the coast of Newfoundland with a boat that was 49 feet, 11 inches long, and he was arrested, dragged into St. John's, and charged. I believe it is wrong to increase the fines in an area that is prohibited to Canadians but open to the Americans.
The Minister said that the nose and the tail of the bank is a Canadian resource. He should explain to the House why Americans are allowed there but Canadians are not. While he may argue that the Americans are not part of NAFO, that does not help Canadian fishermen who know that the Americans are in that area where they are not permitted. It does not help the Newfoundland fishermen to know that the French are overfishing their quota by four, yet no charges are laid because there is a diplomatic dispute between the two countries.
There is only one in 10 foreign boats that have observers. The Minister should explain why he does not put more observers on these foreign boats.
I want to say something about Canadian boats. The inshore fishermen in Newfoundland are now adversely affected three ways: overfishing by foreigners, factory freezer trawlers that were approved by the Government and which gave National Sea Products the boost on the stock market, and the pound quotas now given to Canadian boats. There should be more observers on those large Canadian boats which can presently wash the small fish overboard.
The Government believes this Bill will solve the problem of foreign overfishing by charging Canadians while letting foreigners off scot-free because of a border dispute. That is not good enough in the area where the French overfished its quota by four, and it is not good enough in the nose and tail of the bank where the Americans and everyone else who is not part of NAFO are allowed to fish. This action by the Government is unacceptable.

Mr. Chairman, I listened to the Hon. Member's speech with great interest. When we negotiated at the
Coastal Fisheries Protection Act
Law of the Sea Conference, we gave up the tail and the nose of the bank before we got to the bargaining table. That was discussed long before the present Minister assumed his portfolio. Recently, we were told that during all the surveillance that took place under the Minister who is now in the other place, the observers never saw foreign gear hauled in from the water or saw landed fish in the factory trawler. There was no surveillance.
I agree with the Member that surveillance is still inadequate, but that problem was inherited. I agree that the problem must be addressed, but under no circumstances should the Minister be blamed when observers were not even being put on the boats five years ago. Canadian boats were not being weighed and we were not even estimating the weight of fish that were being taken aboard foreign trawlers.
There is a great foofaraw about what is happening today. The nose and the tail were given away and as a result of the Law of the Sea Conference all those involved with the fishery know that we no longer have the control we want. How it is going to be resolved, I do not know, but blaming the Minister and the Government for an impossible situation which we inherited is not really what I would have expected from the Hon. Member whom I regard so highly and will continue to do so.

Mr. Chairman, this Minister of Fisheries, under the guise of trying to save the stocks on the nose and tail of the banks-and we all want to save the stocks-reached an agreement with the North Atlantic Fisheries Organization, to which so many countries belong, in the last three months, to stop fishing in an area which was considered to be a spawning ground. However, what he forgot in saying that no Canadian boat was allowed to fish there was that the Americans were not a part of NAFO. Perhaps he did not forget. Perhaps he sent his Deputy Minister to have negotiations with the United States. But, to my knowledge, it has not stopped the American fleet from fishing in an area which his Department says we cannot put our boats because it is a NAFO area and the Americans do not belong to NAFO.
Because we gave it away.

The Hon. Member says it is because we gave it away. Well, that area of the banks is right on the line and a little bit outside of the 200 mile zone. There is no doubt about that. However, it is considered internationally to be a Canadian resource. That is why the agreement was made. Where I have extreme difficulty is that the Government tells us that Canadians are not allowed to fish in those areas off the East Coast of Canada but there is nothing we can do about the Americans and any number of other countries because they are not a part of NAFO. I think Canadians on St. Pierre and Miquelon off the South Coast of Newfoundland are just as angry as we are with the Metropolitan Fleet from France. But right is right and wrong is no man's right. We cannot allow a

December 15, 1986
Coastal Fisheries Protection Act
foreign country to overfish a quota by four times with the excuse that we have no control over them, whereas if a Canadian boat went out, that fisherman would be arrested. That is where the Government and I differ.
We do not say the Minister is completely off track but he is certainly not on track as far as being equal and fair. The Minister can stand up and say he cannot control the French in areas 3P or 3J, or whatever one calls it, on the South Coast of Newfoundland. He can say it is in negotiaton. However, if it is in negotiation, we do not hit the poor Canadian boat owner without getting something back from the French and we certainly do not arrest a Canadian boat owner whose boat is right next to an American boat. The American is fishing away and out comes the patrol vessel. The Canadian boat owner is told he is fishing illegally and has to be towed into St. John's, Newfoundland. The Canadian skipper asks about the American right next to him and he is told that the American cannot be touched because he is not a part of NAFO. That is not good enough.

Mr. Chairman, what I think my colleague, the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate, has brought home so vividly here today is the fact that this legislation touches a much broader situation than fisheries management. The Hon. Member mentioned the situation in St. Pierre and Miquelon where the Metropolitan Fleet from France is overfishing and we have no control whatsoever. He mentioned other situations as well. I think the Government and the Minister are badly lacking in fisheries management. I think the fishermen and the people of Canada see that.
The Minister of Fisheries in Nova Scotia reported there is misreporting of catches up to 30 per cent to 50 per cent. 1 do not know how accurate those figures are, but it leaves little for the fishermen in Atlantic Canada and in British Columbia. How can they trust the Government when they hear these stories circulating, particularly when they hear it from provincial Ministers?
This legislation on which we on this side agree-and we will pass it expeditiously today-will not be a panacea to all the ills of the fishery. 1 hope the Minister understands that. It is one thing to have stiffer fines and penalties for foreign overfishing, but how do we enforce those penalties? Since this Government took office we have seen nothing but cuts on the enforcement side of the Department of Fisheries. The Minister mentioned earlier that he was going to expand surveillance and I hope he does. I hope he brings surveillance back to an acceptable level because one reason there is overfishing by foreign fleets is because of the price of fish, which creates a greater demand. I hope the Minister does not believe that by bringing in this legislation it will cure all the ills of the fisheries.
There are many other issues on which we should be speaking when it comes to fish management. There are issues the Government should address very promptly. When the Committee on Fisheries and Oceans travelled to Atlantic Canada, and I see some Hon. Members here who were with us, a number of
issues were put before us by the fishermen. One concern was the problem with the grey seal. I hope when the report on that is made public it will be referred to the Committee on Fisheries and Oceans and dealt with as quickly as possible.
We in the Opposition are prepared to help in any way, shape or form, the Minister and the Government to better manage the fish stocks but I must say it is very disturbing to find out last week or a week and a half ago that the Minister allocated x number of tuna to the Japanese in the St. Margaret Bay area.
I have a letter to the editor of a local newspaper, which I will not read it because it is too long, condemning the Minister and asking for his resignation because of how he handled that situation. I think that was a terrible decision made by the Minister and 1 hope he will learn from that mistake. It is a limited fishery. For the Minister to say it was an experimental long line Japanese fishery is so ludicrous it is not even worth mentioning. There is one thing the tuna fishermen in Prince Edward Island know and that is the keg and line and the fact that a limited number of fishermen have licences to catch tuna. That is one of the reasons there has not been too many tuna caught this year.
I am told by Mr. Robert McFadden, a member of the Atlantic Bluefin Tuna Advisory Committee, that there were nearly 400 tuna caught weighing less than 300 pounds. Good advice for the Minister would be to accept the recommendations of those advisory committees. Certainly when tuna this size is given to a foreign country, it does not say much for the management of the fisheries and the respect fishermen have for that sort of management. While we can be very critical of this, the damage has been done. I hope that it is not repeated in the future by this Minister.
I would like to get the legislation passed today, but I would like to ask the Minister if he intends, along with passing this legislation, to provide for more enforcement and to better manage the fishery resource. This is only the tip of the iceberg. Stiff fines can be imposed but we must be able to catch someone in order to impose those fines.
There are thousands of miles of coastline around Nova Scotia, Newfoundland, Quebec, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. To be fair, I realize that there cannot be a policeman on every corner. However, with these kinds of fines, there will be much more temptation for a sort of hit-and-run type of fishing. We will have to put more teeth in the legislation than the penalties for which it provides. In fact, we will have to back it up with some authority. I hope the Minister is prepared to loosen the purse strings when it comes to enforcement.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to make my response short because we want to get this Bill through the House this afternoon if at all possible. I would point out to the Hon. Member that with the reorganization within the
December 15, 1986

Department which was announced in February and with the regional reorganization that occurred in September, there have been only minor changes to the enforcement contingent. I believe there was a reduction of three out of 700 persons assigned to enforcement duties. However, there have been other increases arising out of funding which was announced in June to embody the various initiatives we are discussing in this debate this afternoon.
I should also point out that some 100 observers are now travelling on foreign vessels in Canadian waters. With the introduction of full cost recovery for observers, we will be adding 100 new observers and they will now be monitoring the fishery on Canadian vessels offshore. We have increased the contingent of observers by some 100 and in fact we are strengthening both the enforcement and the observer functions in this way.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: When shall the Bill be read the third time? By leave, now?
Agreed.

that Bill C-26, an Act to amend the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act, be read the third time and passed.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I would like to rise at this point to offer a summary response to a number of the comments that have been made by my hon. colleagues. I think it is only appropriate that I do this because of some of the particularly forceful assertions which were offered by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker).
It seems from my perspective that the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate is not content with half a bushel. He wants the whole thing. The fact is that when the Party of which he is a member was in Government some 10 years ago, as the Hon. Member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain) has pointed out, the Government did not achieve the control of which the Hon. Member now speaks as being highly desirable in spite of the fact that under international law, such an extension beyond the 200-mile limit would not yet be recognized nor would be feasible in the immediate future.
That in no way negates the benefits to be gained by increasing our ability to police our Fishery at the extremity of the 200-mile fishing limit for those vessels which have been displaced from within the 200-mile limit and hover along the boundary awaiting opportunities to sneak in at night to take fish essentially out of the boats of our own fishermen and the mouths of their children. We are therefore bringing measures
Coastal Fisheries Protection Act
before the House today which will substantially increase the deterrents to foreign fishing within and at the limit of our 200-mile fisheries zone.
I for one would be extremely disappointed if Hon. Members opposite did not support the substantial increases in fines and penalties which are contained within Bill C-26. The spokesman for the Official Opposition has already indicated that support will be forthcoming. I think it is particularly significant that he has said that because, as we celebrate the tenth anniversary of Canada's assertion of the 200-mile exclusive fishing zone, we are raising the fines for illegal fishing without a licence within Canadian waters from $100,000 to $750,000 maximum on indictment, an increase of seven and a half times.
We will increase the fine for convictions of illegal fishing by summary conviction from $25,000 to $150,000, a sixfold increase. For other offences, a number of which are set out in the Sections of the present Coastal Fisheries Protection Act and its regulations including evading arrest and failing to stop when commanded, fines under indictment will be increased from $25,000 to $500,000, an increase of 20 times. For summary conviction offences of the same nature, the fines will be increased from a maximum of $5,000 to a maximum of $100,000, an increase of some 20 times.
Why are these increased fines necessary? In the past three or four years, as we have displaced foreign fishing vessels from within our 200-mile limit to the very rich extremities of the Grand Bank known as the nose and tail of the Bank, we have seen a very rapid escalation in illegal fishing along the line of and within the Canadian 200-mile zone. The result of that is that in 1984, there were 49 detected violations and seven convictions. Total fines of $8,000 were imposed and the average fine was $1,000. That was the situation in 1984.
In 1985 there was a virtual doubling of violations from 49 to 90. In 1985 we collected fines of $1.25 million with an average fine of $56,000. Comparing those fines with the levels that we are discussing today, we can see how important this additional deterrence will be. Already in 1986 we have had 48 violations, but at this time in the year that represents a substantial reduction from the number of violations recorded in 1985. So far this year $286,000 in fines have been levied with an average fine of $25,000, and $46,000 in forfeitures of catch.
The principles embodied in this Bill are to give effect to the various measures announced in a speech I gave in St. John's, Newfoundland, on Friday, June 13. At that time, I indicated that we would substantially increase our ability to detect violations, and that we would substantially increase our ability to chase and apprehend violators. All of that would be of little significance if we then did not have the legal provision to essentially throw the book at those who would offend against our exclusive fishing zone. That is why it is essential that these significant increases in penalty be approved today.

December 15, 1986
Adjournment Debate
I spoke earlier at the committee stage about our decision to arm our offshore patrol vessels, of which there are five operating on the Atlantic coast, with light machine-gun armaments, and to ensure that those armaments are used according to rules of engagement, so that we are in no way seen to be irresponsible or unduly antagonistic. However, we must show foreign nations, including the United States, and vessels of any other foreign origin, that Canadian fish stocks within our fishing zone are to first benefit our Canadian fishing communities and fishermen.
Hon. Members have spoken about certain complications where, as a member of the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries Organization, we enter into arrangements with foreign countries that recognize Canada's authority to manage these fish stocks, both within and beyond the 200-mile limit. In exchange for their co-operation, they are allowed to fish for surplus stocks within the Canadian zone. At the same time, we expect their full co-operation on conservation measures on the nose and tail of the Grand Banks.
Unfortunately, as the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillin-gate has indicated, there are certain complications. There are unresolved questions of allocation to the French Metropolitan Fleet which are presently being discussed at the diplomatic level, as the Hon. Member well knows. There is the problem of overfishing by that French fleet in area 3PS which surrounds the islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon. Something has to be done to bring under control that blatant abuse of resources which we believe to be Canadian. Next year the long-term agreement expires with the European nations, the Economic Community. Under our policy that allocation which the European nations have enjoyed will not be renewed. But there is also a problem with the American vessels, as the Member for Gander-Twillingate has pointed out.
Since The Hague line was established, conveying to Canada a greater portion of the rich fish stocks on Georges Bank, some of the U.S. vessels that formerly fished in an area which is now part of the Canadian Fisheries zone are fishing on the tail of the Grand Banks. They are not fishing for our prime cod stocks, but they are indeed fishing for flat-fish or flounder.
Diplomatic initiatives must be continued to encourage the Americans to fish responsibly and not to abuse our stocks, as well as all of the other countries that will be subject to the fines established under this legislation.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for your co-operation and that of all Members. I am sure that their good sense will persuade them to support this very important and positive initiative on behalf of the fishermen of Atlantic Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I know that I only have a couple of minutes. The fact is that today the Minister has decreased the quotas for Canadian fishermen on the East Coast. They have been decreased for groundfish. At the same time it is recognized, as the Minister just did, that the French Metropolitan Fleet is overfishing by four times what it is allowed in that entire area off the coast of
Newfoundland and off the east coast of Nova Scotia. After we agreed for conservation purposes with NAFO to cut out our fishing on the tail of the bank, the Americans moved in with their fleet. The Minister says that there is nothing he can legally do about that.
The Canadian quotas are cut back. If they fish any more than their quota, they are arrested and will receive big fines. The fishermen will never get out of jail. Yet the French fleet is overfishing all it wants. The Americans are on the tail of the bank overfishing all they want. Right next to them are the Canadians who will be arrested and given these great new fines. The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) has admitted, and he is absolutely correct, that right now the Canadian Government cannot do anything about the foreign fleets. Yet the Canadian quotas have been reduced for groundfish off the East Coast.
What we are saying to the federal Government today is to beware. Canadian fishermen will not put up with this much longer. They will not accept that double standard that is being presented to them by this Government. They are not going to take it, and they will show their displeasure with this Government when the next election rolls around.

Mr. Speaker, very briefly, so that we can get this Bill through, I wish to indicate our support for the measures the Government is taking in increasing the fines that will be levied against foreign vessels which transgress Canadian fisheries regulations, and Canadian vessels which pick up any foreign catches. That is important. The previous Member who spoke did not mean to indicate that Canadian fishermen will be hit with these high fines, because that is not the way the Bill reads, as I understand it. I stand to be corrected if the Member is correct.
These measures are important. I urge the Government to continue to take a strong position vis-a-vis France and the United States and get them to respect Canadian rights and Canadian conservation measures in these waters. Again, I am happy to give my support for these measures.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the third time and passed.
A motion to adjourn the House under Standing Order 66 deemed to have been moved.

subtopic: DISARMAMENT-UNITED STATES STRATEGIC DEFENSE INITIATIVE-GOVERNMENT POSITION. (B) RESEARCH UNDERTAKEN BY UNITED STATES
DISARMAMENT-UNITED STATES STRATEGIC DEFENSE INITIATIVE-GOVERNMENT POSITION. (B) RESEARCH UNDERTAKEN BY UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, these proceedings arise out of a question I put to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) right after the collapse of the Reykjavik Summit. That summit fell apart because President Reagan rejected a
December 15, 1986

Soviet offer to cut offensive nuclear missiles and keep star wars research in the laboratory for 10 years. Instead, President Reagan wishes to deploy a ballistic missile defence system after 10 years of development.
I asked my question for the reason that President Reagan's position flatly contradicted Canadian Government policy. That policy was set out by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) in the House on January 23. It can be summed up in one sentence:
Our stance toward SDI research is rooted in the need to conform strictly with the provisions of the ABM treaty.
Article V of that treaty reads as follows:
Each party undertakes not to develop, test, or deploy ABM systems or components which are sea-based, air-based, space-based or mobile land-based.
Clearly the Government could no longer support President Reagan. He wanted development and deployment, which is explicitly forbidden. I was therefore astounded when the Prime Minister asserted that his Government's policy was still in effect. How could this be?
We found out when the Secretary of State for External Affairs returned from Europe. He told the House that the summit had been a great success. The only thing left to work out, according to the Minister, was the definition of research. He said that should be left to American and Soviet negotiators.
The Secretary did a great disservice to the country. Canadian lives are at risk, and they will suffer the consequences of another arms race. The Government has a responsibility to speak out for them. He also conveniently ignored the fact that his Government's policy rested on a Canadian interpretation of star wars and the ABM treaty.
Let us look at how the Americans see that treaty. Paul Nitze, the President's special adviser on arms control, told a New York audience on October 31:
The restrictions of Article V of the treaty do not apply to ABM systems based on other physical principles and their components.
He went on to say:
The United States need not accept limitations on permitted development and testing activities.
In a nutshell, the Canadian Government says it will support star wars only if research conforms strictly with the ABM treaty, and the Americans say they can and will ignore that treaty. Therefore, the Government can no longer support star wars.
Reykjavik should have crushed any illusions that the Government had about star wars. The House will remember that the Government began by defending SDI as prudent research to keep up with the Soviet Union. However, prudent research is exactly what President Reagan turned down by refusing to keep research in the laboratory for 10 years.
Adjournment Debate
Neither is star wars a bargaining chip. Some argued that star wars would bring the Soviets back to the bargaining table. However, when Mr. Gorbachev came and made the concessions in offensive arms which the West had been seeking for years, President Reagan would not bargain. Instead he wanted to deploy his "insurance policy". Finally, the Secretary of State for External Affairs argued that star wars could be the subject of negotiation under the ABM treaty. However, Mr. Nitze's statements make it clear that the Americans will not accept limits on SDI.
It has come down to a choice between star wars and arms control. SDI is riding roughshod over existing arms control treaties, and it is preventing new agreements from being signed.
In conclusion, Canada must now say no to star wars. A responsible friend and ally would tell the United States that breaking treaties and passing up the chance for arms reductions is not in anyone's best interests.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DISARMAMENT-UNITED STATES STRATEGIC DEFENSE INITIATIVE-GOVERNMENT POSITION. (B) RESEARCH UNDERTAKEN BY UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the Hon. Member knows that SDI is a research program concerning various ABM defence concepts. The technical feasibility of such a project can be ascertained only after further research which will be completed in the early 1990s, if ever.
The Government supports this research program which it views as a precautionary measure warranted by the existence of a similar program in the U.S.S.R. For a number of years now the Soviets have been doing extensive ABM defence research at centres such as Sary Shagan. In addition, both superpowers should indeed consider the possibility of jointly and progressively abandoning a deterrent, system based on guaranteed mutual destruction through offensive nuclear weapons and opt instead for defensive systems combined with reduced arsenals of offensive weapons.
This was the position of the American negotiators at the Geneva discussions on nuclear and space armament, and we supported it.
Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that SDI has something to do with the U.S.S.R. returning to the Geneva negotiation table and the more pragmatic approach taken by the Soviets in recent months. It is unfortunate that at Reykjavik Mr. Gorbachev unilaterally chose to make the SDI interruption a prerequisite of progress in other sectors of nuclear armament control.
The Hon. Member for Brant was wondering about a connection between SDI and the ABM missile treaty. Had he quoted Article V of the treaty in extenso he would have realized that both signatories to the treaty have undertaken not to develop, test, or deploy ABM systems or components which are sea-based, air-based, space-based or mobile land-based.

December 15, 1986
Adjournment Debate
However, the Treaty authorizes the development and deployment of a fixed land system as well as research on all types of systems.
In Reykjavik, Soviet Secretary General Gorbachev however added a new dimension to the discussions by requiring that all research on anti-missile defence systems be carried out only in laboratories, which would go beyond the restrictions contained in Clause V of the Treaty. Indeed, the word "laboratory" is not even mentioned in the Treaty, much less defined.
Has my allotted time expired, Mr. Speaker?

subtopic: PURCHASE OF CANADIAN PACIFIC AIRLINES BY PACIFIC WESTERN AIRLINES. (B) MINISTER'S POSITION.
PURCHASE OF CANADIAN PACIFIC AIRLINES BY PACIFIC WESTERN AIRLINES. (B) MINISTER'S POSITION.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 3 of this year, in a question to the Minister of Transport, I raised the matter of the sale of CP Air to Pacific Western Airlines of Calgary. I asked the question because we Liberals, like so many Canadians, are very concerned about the increasing concentration of power in the air transport industry. If this sale is approved by the Canadian Transport Commission, it will be the seventh major takeover in Canada in less than two years. This sale, if it is approved, will put Canada in a situation where two carriers control 90 per cent of the air traffic in this country.
In the circumstances, we might have expected an entirely different answer from the Minister, because we can hardly take lightly a matter that is causing considerable concern to workers in the transport industry as well as to users of the services offered by our Canadian airlines.
The Minister said, and I quote, at page 1736 of Hansard'.
-I think that Canada will be better served by having two healthy competitors than by having the giant Air Canada and a group of financially weak or regionally small airlines. We will have both. We will have two large competitive national airlines and a plethora of smaller regional and local airlines.
Unfortunately for the Minister and perhaps more importantly for Canadians, the Minister's analysis does not stand the test of scrutiny. Indeed, how can the Minister suggest that following the sale we would have the best of both worlds, in effect, two large carriers competing with small regional airlines when in fact over the last two years seven major takeovers have concentrated 90 per cent of traffic in the hands of two carriers? Surely the Minister cannot be suggesting that what we are experiencing today in Canada is competition in any meaningful sense of the word. Surely the Minister is well aware that, in fact, what we are experiencing is concentration of ownership in fewer and fewer hands, a situation that is becoming very serious, having to deal with the disappearance of more and more regional carriers with the resulting loss in employment and service all across Canada.
I spoke earlier about the concern of airline industry workers over the effect this purchase and sale might have on their jobs. They had expected, quite legitimately, that the Minister would offer assurances that this sale, if approved, would not result in any loss of employment. In fact, news of the purchase was immediately condemned by leaders of the Brotherhood of Railway and Airline Clerks who are afraid job losses will occur. I regret that the Minister ignored their fear and has not addressed it in the House. Neither has he addressed the eventual loss of service for the region.
[ Translation]
It is a foregone conclusion that Canadian Pacific and Pacific Western, which cover about the same territory in Western Canada, will no longer compete for those routes in the future. It is also clear that the new company will see to it that routes are rationalized, so that the travelling public in Western Canada, which up to now has had a choice of airlines, will no longer have that option in the future, the result being higher prices and all the other consequences of such an arrangement.
What I find surprising at this point is that despite the assurances we were given a few months ago by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs when the new competition legislation was adopted in the House, no information or prior notice was given the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs regarding this takeover. This means that we on this side of the House were misled by the Canadian Government when it told us it was putting in place new competition legislation that would prevent takeovers if the impact would be to substantially reduce competition. Indeed the new competition legislation has yet to be enforced, and a takeover which may have dire consequences on Canadian air transport can become reality without monitoring on the part of both the Minister of Transport, who seems to be rejoicing at this takeover, and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, who did not have the nerve to ensure that his legislation was in force and who failed to take appropriate steps to compel Pacific Western to give the Director of Investigation and Research on combines due notice of this takeover before it was finalized.
I am asking the Minister to take another look at this file and make sure that Canada will still have two major air carriers as we had before, as well as six or seven large regional carriers and lots of small local carriers.
Such was the situation before the Conservatives came to power, but it is deteriorating at the very moment when the Government is talking about deregulation legislation which is supposed to increase competitiveness and rejuvenate the air transport market. I think the Conservative Government is treating the population as fools. I realize that we are getting close to Christmas, but the fool in all this is the Minister of Transport, not the Canadian people.
December 15, 1986

speakeroldname: Mr. J. M. Forrestall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion
subtopic: PURCHASE OF CANADIAN PACIFIC AIRLINES BY PACIFIC WESTERN AIRLINES. (B) MINISTER'S POSITION.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) and his Party who treated Canadians as fools. He sits in his place and says certain things are being done and ignores other facts. The fact is that there is ample opportunity for recourse.
The Member rose to his feet on December 3 and asked the Minister to intervene, rescind and disallow. The fact is there are laws and regulations in this country. I do not know why the former Minister, as knowledgeable as he sometimes seems to be, would not know that. Section 27 of the National Transportation Act stipulates that any air carrier which proposes to acquire another transportation system must give notice to the CTC, which in turn must give notice to the public. The Member is a former Minister and he knows that. The CTC may receive objections, investigate and may hold public hearings if it considers such hearings to be necessary or desirable and in the public interest.
The CTC may intervene of its own accord. It does not need an objection, as the Hon. Member knows. In either case, the CTC is empowered to disallow, of its own authority and by its own experience, that of which the Hon. Member expresses concern and says we have no capacity with respect to.
The CTC's decision on this matter may be appealed to the Cabinet under Section 64 of the NTA. In addition, the very powerful provisions covering mergers in the new Competition Act apply to transactions such as PWA's purchase of CPAL. The Member for Papineau knows that. I wonder what is after with his smoke and mirrors act.
The CTC has a considerable degree of independence from the Government and it would be both premature and inappropriate for any Minister, let alone this Minister, to directly or indirectly intervene in this decision-making process.
The matter will go through the process. If there are objections, they will be lodged with the appropriate authority. If the CTC deems it necessary, as I expect it will, it will call public hearings and that will be the end of the matter. Due process will prevail. The Member's instructions to the Government to intervene are inappropriate and simply not acceptable, as he knows.

subtopic: NATIONAL RESEARCH COUNCIL-SIZE OF BUDGET AND STAFF. (B) BUDGETARY CUT-BACKS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
NATIONAL RESEARCH COUNCIL-SIZE OF BUDGET AND STAFF. (B) BUDGETARY CUT-BACKS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the middle of October when the Minister of Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle) made his somewhat infamous statement that there are no cuts at the National Research Council, it really stretched the credulity of Canadians across the country. It was a bit like the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) saying he had nothing to do with putting a prison in his riding. We had to find the truth from another source.
Adjournment Debate
At the press conference given by the President of the National Research Council, Dr. Larkin Kerwin, he said it would be much more difficult to avoid lay-offs with this round of cuts than with the previous round. You will recall that after the Government took office in 1984, 400 positions were eliminated at the National Research Council. Through various techniques such as a hiring freeze, early retirement and reassignment of personnel within the NRC, the Council was able to avoid all but a few lay-offs. However, Dr. Kerwin admitted that the fat had been cut and that it would be much harder to avoid lay-offs with the 200 positions which must be cut by next April 1 on the orders of the Government.
The truth is that it is ridiculous to suggest that you can recycle highly specialized scientists. Several weeks ago there was a front-page article in The Financial Post which quoted, among others, a researcher at the National Research Council who said that suggesting that one can recycle a scientist who has dedicated his life to work in a particular field was like telling a heart surgeon that from now on he can only operate on kidneys.
The truth was told by Dr. Basinski, a recipient of the Order of Canada, who has been told that he can remain with only one technician. He is losing the rest of his staff and support personnel. He indicated that under those circumstances it would probably be a waste of his time and of taxpayers' money for him to continue. The truth is that morale has never been so low as it is at the National Research Council under the policies of the Government.
I recall speaking to a scientist recently who told me that even if the cuts were reversed today, he is not sure he would want to remain at the NRC, which he regards as more of a liability than an asset to him at this time in his career.
How did we get into this sorry state of affairs? Denny Doyle, a member of the outside Council, perhaps provided a small explanation when he told our committee several weeks ago that at his behest, the NRC prepared a five-year plan after the cuts in 1984. He felt that the best way to let the Government know about the NRC's plans was to put it down on paper and give the Government an opportunity to react. If there was any disagreement with what the NRC was doing, presumably the Government, through the Minister, would say so.
The Minister of State for Science and Technology is proud to say that as one of his first actions he endorsed the five-year plan. He has repeated this endlessly, yet in one breath he endorses the plan, then asks the NRC to cut another $20 million from its budget. Is it surprising that Mr. Doyle said to our committee that he is really not sure what the shareholder, meaning the Government, wants from the NRC.
1 want to be very clear. I am not saying that there should be no changes at the National Research Council, but changes should be justified and should be implemented in an orderly fashion, in a process that is rigorous and respected. This has not happened at the NRC.

December 15, 1986
Adjournment Debate
I can give several further examples. For instance, I can point to the recommendations of the Wright Report that were published in July, 1984. To date, there has been no formal response by the Government to this examination of government policies and programs for technology development.
In August, 1985, the former Minister of Science and Technology asked for the views of the Science Council of Canada on how the Government might implement the recommendations of the task force. In September, 1985, the Science Council recommended that a review of government labs be undertaken by an agency at arm's length to the Government. Such a review should be thorough, fair, comprehensive and forward looking. To be successful, the review would need the support and interest of government scientists and engineers and the clients of the labs, and therefore should include interviews with them.
Fifteen months have gone by since the Science Council of Canada made these recommendations and no apparent response has yet been given by the Government.
I am suggesting that the National Research Council is operating in a policy vacuum. It does not know what is expected of it because it has not been told by its political masters. Canadians deserve a detailed statement of government policy with respect to the National Research Council and government labs. Until such time, the cuts that were announced by the Government in October should be rescinded.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gordon Towers (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: NATIONAL RESEARCH COUNCIL-SIZE OF BUDGET AND STAFF. (B) BUDGETARY CUT-BACKS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the National Research Council is the single largest research body in Canada. The Government has new priorities for science and technology and it is only natural that there be a re-evaluation of individual government programs, including those within the NRC.
When programs which may have been justifiable within the context of past objectives are re-examined in terms of new priorities, some are found to be inappropriate. They are discontinued. These decisions cannot be considered cuts if, at
the same time, other programs are expanded and initiated. This is what is happening in NRC.
Between 1984-85 and 1987-88 the budget of NRC will fall by about $50 million. However, all but $10 million of this reduction is accounted for by less construction. Research contributions, salaries and operating costs have not fallen significantly so that in total, the effective program at NRC is not reduced. Of course, some programs have been discontinued. At the same time, there are offsetting increases in biotechnology and other areas which will approximately equal these recent reductions.
Driving this reallocation of priorities within NRC is the Government's view of Canadian science and technology. This view is still being hammered out in discussions with provincial, university and industry representatives and significant announcements will soon be made. The Speech from the Throne outlined a renewed commitment by the federal Government to science and technology in Canada and announced several initiatives such as a national advisory board on industrial technology to be chaired by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), the introduction of a federal science and technology strategy and the establishment of a Canadian space agency. Some of the Government's intentions are clear and have influenced decisions made at NRC and elsewhere. The reallocation of work at NRC and other Government laboratories is taking place in the context of an expanded role for university and industry researchers. The expansion in external research will be the foundation for a sustained increase in total research and development in the future.
As the Minister has often stated, Canada must move into the 21st century in so far as research, science and technology is concerned.
